cards.name: the Wave Code letters
cards.pat: \bwhat (does|do|is) (the |my )?(letter )?(q|s|f|t|d|n|e|a)( (mean|means|stand|stands|in|for|letter)\b|$)|\b(letters?|quick spark|slow simmer|nuanced|explicit|attuned)\b[^?]*\b(wave ?codes?|wavelength)\b|\b(wave ?codes?|wavelength)\b[^?]*\b(letters?|quick spark|slow simmer|nuanced|explicit|attuned)\b|\bwhat (is|are|does) (a |my |the )?wave ?codes?( mean)?\b|\b(quick spark|slow simmer)\b
what: Your Wave Code is four letters from Wavelength, one for each part. It’s a bit like the four-letter personality types you may have seen, but it’s a fun way to describe your preferences, not a test that measures you. Everyone uses both ends of each line sometimes.
Here’s what each letter means:
how: Q, Quick Spark (pace): you think fast and out loud, and ideas show up mid-sentence. The gift is energy and momentum. To tune in to a Q: let them think aloud without treating every idea as a final answer.

S, Slow Simmer (pace): you process inside before speaking, and the good thoughts often arrive later. The gift is depth and steadiness. To tune in to an S: give a heads-up before big talks, and accept “I need time to think” as a real answer.
F, Forest (lens): you see the big picture first: patterns, purpose and how it all connects. The gift is vision. To tune in to an F: start with the why, then help with the steps.
T, Trees (lens): you start with the specifics: steps, facts and exact details. The gift is precision and follow-through. To tune in to a T: be concrete. “Saturday at 10” beats “sometime soon.”
D, Direct (sending): you say it plainly, and honesty is how you show respect. The gift is clarity. To tune in to a D: listen to the words, not an imagined tone. Bluntness usually isn’t anger.
N, Nuanced (sending): you cushion what you say and read the moment, and may hint first. The gift is tact and warmth. To tune in to an N: make it safe to be direct, and take soft hints seriously.
E, Explicit (receiving): you take words at face value and want things spelled out. The gift is clear agreements. To tune in to an E: say exactly what you mean, without counting on hints or sarcasm.
A, Attuned (receiving): you read tone, mood and what’s under the words. The gift is empathy. To tune in to an A: mind your tone, and say so when you’re stressed about something else.
cards.pillar: Together the four letters make one of 16 archetypes, like the Firefly (QFNA) or the Compass (STDE). Want the list?

links: The four letters on one page

what: Your four Wave Code letters make one of 16 Wavelength archetypes. Each is a picture of how you tend to think, talk and listen, not a box. Here they are:
how: QFDE, the Comet: fast, visionary and straight-talking. Wants the same honesty back.
QFDA, the Sunflare: bursting with big ideas and blunt about them, yet feels every shift in tone.
QFNE, the Kite: quick, imaginative and gentle with words. Needs things said plainly in return.
QFNA, the Firefly: bright, warm, full of ideas, and quick to sense how others feel.
QTDE, the Hummingbird: fast, precise and to the point. Clear in, clear out.
QTDA, the Spark Plug: gets things moving and says what’s needed, but tone lands deep.
QTNE, the Bumblebee: busy, practical and kind in delivery. Likes instructions spelled out.
QTNA, the Otter: quick, hands-on, playful, and always reading the room.
SFDE, the Owl: thinks long and deep, speaks plainly, and takes words at face value.
SFDA, the Lighthouse: steady, far-seeing and honest, with a keen sense for the mood around them.
SFNE, the Tide: slow and deep, gentle in delivery, and grateful for clear, direct words.
SFNA, the Willow: reflective and soft-spoken. Feels the undercurrents of every room.
STDE, the Compass: steady, exact and direct. Wants clear words and clear plans.
STDA, the Oak: steady and practical, honest in what they say, sensitive to how it’s said back.
STNE, the Hearth: calm, careful and kind. Does best when expectations are spelled out.
STNA, the Quilt: patient, detail-minded and gentle. Stitches people together by noticing everything.
cards.pillar: On your results, Wavelength adds what you bring at your best, what to watch for, and how someone can tune in to each letter.

what: In Wavelength, the wiring step is optional, and you can select all that apply: Neurotypical, ADHD, Autistic, Dyslexic, Highly sensitive, Not sure yet, or Something else (with a box to name it). ADHD and Autistic together is often called AuDHD, and Wavelength says so. Your wiring only decides which options you see first in each part, and “Show options from other wiring types” opens the rest.

It’s self-identified, so no diagnosis is needed, and Wavelength is not a diagnosis or a test that measures you. If you’re not sure, the “Not sure which fits?” guide explains each type, with “you might relate if” examples and a “That’s me” button. If you’re curious about a formal assessment, a doctor or psychologist can help.
how: Open Wavelength and tap Start. The wiring step comes first.
Tap every type that fits you, or skip it. Picking “Not sure yet” shows options from every type.
Read the short explanation under your picks, or the guide below them if you need help.
Change it anytime with “Change my wiring” on your results.
cards.pillar: Your wiring shapes how you send and receive, which is Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: the 9 inputs of learning
cards.pat: \b(nine|9) inputs\b|\binputs? of learning\b|\blearning inputs?\b|\binputs?\b[^?]*\bwavelength\b|\bwavelength\b[^?]*\binputs?\b|\bstrongest input\b
what: The 9 inputs of learning are the ways people take in the world and make things click. Wavelength asks you to tap every one that helps you, then pick your strongest. They’re adapted from Howard Gardner’s idea of multiple intelligences. Treat them as preferences, not fixed learning styles: research doesn’t support learning through only one style, and most people learn best when several work together.
Here are the nine:
how: 💬 Words: talking, reading, writing and stories.
🔢 Logic and numbers: reasons, rules, numbers and how things work.
🖼️ Pictures and space: images, diagrams, color, maps and where things are.
🤲 Hands and movement: doing, touching, moving and making.
🎵 Sound and rhythm: tone, music, rhythm and how things sound.
🤝 People: learning with others and reading how they feel.
🌙 Inner reflection: quiet thinking, journaling and knowing yourself.
🌿 Nature and patterns: noticing, sorting and reading environments.
✨ Big questions and meaning: purpose, values and the why behind everything.
cards.pillar: Each input has its own self-discovery chapter, and “How the 9 inputs connect” maps their links in five levels, from obvious (words and people: conversation) to the deepest (hands and people: care sent through actions often goes unseen by a words-first partner), with three flowcharts and a nine-point check before a hard conversation.

Nine for the inputs of learning: one for each input, from learning through words to learning through big questions and meaning, each with how it connects to the others.
Your journal answers stay in your browser. They’re kept on this device only if you tick “Keep my answers and journal on this device,” and “Copy my journal” copies them all.

cards.name: comparing Wave Codes
cards.pat: \bcompar\w*\b[^?]*\b(wave ?codes?|wavelength)\b|\b(both|two|our) wave ?codes?\b
what: To compare in Wavelength, the other person takes it too (on their own device, so their answers stay theirs) and tells you their four-letter Wave Code. On your results, type it under “Compare with someone.” You’ll see both archetypes, how many letters you share, and a tip for each of the four lines: pace, lens, sending and receiving.
how: Same letter: that part usually runs smoothly, with a tip for keeping it that way.
Q and S: the Quick Spark can say “I’m just brainstorming,” and the Slow Simmer can say “I’ll come back to this by tonight.”
F and T: start with the big picture, then agree on the first concrete step together.
D and N: agree that plain words aren’t anger, and soft words still count.
E and A: say what you mean, and say it kindly. Here, both matter.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive: a mismatch is something to tune, not a fault in either of you.

what: I can’t tell you that, and I won’t guess. I can’t diagnose anyone, and nobody can from a chat, least of all someone who isn’t here to speak for themselves. A label also matters less than what actually happens between you.
how: Look at the pattern, not the label: what do they do, how often, and how do you feel around them?
Notice whether it’s new or has always been there, and whether it’s getting worse.
If you’re worried about their health, say so kindly and suggest they see their doctor. A doctor or psychologist is the right person to assess it.
If you feel scared, controlled or put down, that matters more than any label: the Not safe at home? page lists the signs, and people to talk to.
For yourself, a counsellor can help you think it through, whatever the answer turns out to be.
script: I’ve noticed you’ve seemed really up and down lately, and I’m worried about you. Would you talk to your doctor about it? I’ll come with you if you like.

what: I can’t tell you that, and I won’t guess: nobody can diagnose PTSD from a chat. What you describe, waking up and jumping at noises, is common after a deployment or anything frightening. It isn’t a weakness, and it’s worth raising with a doctor. Help tends to work better when it starts early.
how: Start with your doctor or GP: tell them about the sleep and the jumpiness, and how long it has been going on.
US service members and veterans: call 988, then press 1, any time. Military OneSource is free and confidential on 800-342-9647.
UK veterans: the Combat Stress helpline is 0800 138 1619.
Meanwhile, make a pause plan together while things are calm: a word that means “I need a break”, and a time you’ll come back.

what: Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean, usually as a joke or to show annoyance. The words say one thing and the tone says another: “Oh great, that’s just perfect” after something goes wrong means it isn’t great.
how: Look for a mismatch: positive words about something that has just gone badly.
Listen for the tone: flatter, slower or extra bright, sometimes with an eye-roll.
Use the context: if the thing just went wrong, “great” probably isn’t praise.
If you can’t tell, it’s fair to ask. Many autistic people find sarcasm confusing, and asking is a good skill, not a failing.
script: Sorry, I take words at face value. Was that a joke, or do you mean it?
links: Three channels, tuned differently (tone, words and context)

cards.name: a meltdown or a tantrum?
cards.pat: \b(difference|different|differ)\b.{0,30}\bmeltdowns?\b.{0,25}\btantrums?\b|\b(difference|different)\b.{0,30}\btantrums?\b.{0,25}\bmeltdowns?\b|\bmeltdowns?\b.{0,20}\b(and|or|vs|versus)\b.{0,10}\b(a )?tantrums?\b|\bis (a |it a )?meltdown (just )?(a )?tantrum\b|\bare meltdowns (just )?tantrums\b
what: A tantrum is usually aimed at getting something, and it can stop when that happens. A meltdown has no goal: it’s an overwhelmed nervous system losing control, and it stops when the overwhelm passes. A meltdown is closer to something that happens to a person than something they do.
how: A meltdown is outward: crying, shouting, running or lashing out. A shutdown is the quiet version: going still or silent.
A meltdown needs safety, quiet and time, not consequences.
A tantrum often eases when an adult stays calm and close, without giving in.
Afterwards, look for the cause: noise, tiredness, a change, or too much at once.

what: I can’t tell you that, and I won’t guess. I can’t diagnose anyone, and nobody can tell from a chat. A clinician can, and asking is a sensible step, not a big drama.

cards.name: your nervous system
cards.pat: \b(what is|what s|whats|explain|how does|tell me about|what does) (the |my |your |our )?(nervous system|vagus nerve|vagal tone|stress response|autonomic nervous system)\b|\b(calm|reset|regulate|soothe|settle) (my|your|the|our) (nervous system|vagus nerve)\b|\b(nervous system|vagus nerve) (reset|regulation|hacks?|exercises?|stimulation)\b|\b(dysregulated|dysregulation|my nervous system is)\b|\bfight,? flight,? (or |and )?(freeze|fawn)\b|\bfight or flight\b|\bwhat is fawning\b|\binteroception\b|\bpolyvagal\b
what: Your nervous system is how your body notices things, reacts and settles again. It has a “go” side and a “rest” side, and you need both. Feeling wired, frozen or flat is your nervous system doing its job, sometimes a bit too well.

What helps it settle: a longer out-breath, movement, cool water on the face, a safe person, and sleep. Popular ideas such as polyvagal theory and “fawning” give useful words, but they aren’t settled science.
how: Breathe out longer than you breathe in: in for 4, out for 6, for a minute or two.
Move for a few minutes: walk, climb the stairs, shake out your arms.
Cool your face with cold water for up to 30 seconds (skip it if you have a heart condition).
If panic, feeling unreal or low mood keeps coming back, see a doctor.
links: Your nervous system, in plain words

cards.name: something calming

what: Of course. Let’s slow down together for a moment.
how: Let your shoulders drop, and unclench your jaw.
Breathe in gently for a count of four, then out slowly for a count of six. Do that three times.
Nothing needs deciding in the next few minutes. You’re allowed to just be here.
For a guided breathing break, the breathing pacer on Upset right now? breathes with you, in for 4 and out for 6.

what: I’m glad you asked. When panic won’t stop, or you’ve felt low for weeks, that’s more than a supplement can fix, and you deserve real help from a person.

In the US you can call or text 988 any time. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans are free on 116 123. If you might be in danger right now, call 911 or 999. Your doctor can help too, and it’s worth telling them about any herbs or supplements you take.
links: Getting help: when it’s more than everyday stress

cards.name: St John’s wort and other medicines
cards.pat: \b(st|saint) johns? ?s? ?wort\b
what: Please don’t take it with an antidepressant without talking to your prescriber or pharmacist first. St John’s wort can clash with antidepressants such as SSRIs and cause serotonin syndrome, which can be dangerous.

It also stops birth control pills working properly, and affects blood thinners, HIV and transplant medicines. And never stop an antidepressant suddenly to switch. A pharmacist can check everything you take.
links: St John’s wort: what the research says

cards.name: ashwagandha
cards.pat: \bashwagandha\b
what: Small studies suggest ashwagandha may ease stress a little, but there are real safety warnings: rare liver injury has been reported, it may affect the thyroid, and there are concerns in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Denmark banned it in food supplements in 2023.
Please check with a pharmacist or doctor before taking it, especially alongside other medicines.

cards.name: kava
cards.pat: \bkava\b
what: Kava may ease anxiety slightly, but it has been linked to rare, serious liver damage, including deaths. Never mix it with alcohol, or with sleeping or anxiety medicines. Most people are better off choosing something safer.
Please talk to a pharmacist or doctor first.

cards.name: melatonin
cards.pat: \bmelatonin\b
what: Melatonin is for sleep timing, such as jet lag or shift work, not for anxiety, and guidelines advise against it for long-term insomnia. In the UK it is a prescription medicine; in the US it is sold as a supplement, and the amount in the bottle can differ from the label.
I can’t advise on amounts. For children, talk to a doctor first; for adults, ask a pharmacist or doctor, especially alongside other medicines.

cards.name: chamomile
cards.pat: \bchamomile\b
what: Maybe a little. A few small studies hint that chamomile may ease long-running worry, but the evidence is early, and it hasn’t been shown to help sleep.
As a tea it is likely safe, unless you are allergic to ragweed or related plants, or take warfarin. If you take other medicines, check with a pharmacist or doctor.

cards.name: magnesium
cards.pat: \bmagnesium\b
what: The research is weak: some small studies found a benefit for anxiety or sleep, but reviewers called the evidence poor quality. Too much from supplements causes diarrhea, and it isn’t right for everyone, for example with kidney problems.
Please check with a pharmacist or doctor before taking it, especially alongside other medicines.

cards.name: CBD
cards.pat: \b(cbd|cannabidiol)\b
what: There is little good research on CBD for everyday stress or anxiety so far. The only approved CBD medicine in the US is a purified prescription form for seizures linked to three rare conditions: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, Dravet syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex. The FDA warns CBD can harm the liver and change how other medicines work, including antidepressants and blood thinners.
Please check with a pharmacist or doctor first.

cards.name: homeopathy
cards.pat: \bhomeopath\w*\b
what: There is no good-quality evidence that homeopathy works for any health condition. If you use it, please don’t let it replace treatment that works, and tell your doctor or pharmacist what you take.

I take sertraline and I’m thinking of trying St John’s wort. Is that safe together?
I’ve been taking ashwagandha for stress. Should I keep going, and do I need a blood test?

cards.name: are supplements and herbs safe, and mixing them with medicines
cards.pat: \b(are|is) (supplements?|herbs?|herbal (remedies|supplements?|teas?)|natural remed\w*|natural supplements?)\b.{0,15}\b(safe|dangerous|ok|okay|regulated|tested)\b|\b(mix|mixing|take|taking|combine|combining)\b.{0,25}\b(herbs?|herbal \w+|supplements?|natural remed\w*)\b.{0,25}\b(with|and|alongside)\b.{0,25}\b(medication|medicine|meds|pills?|prescription|antidepressants?|sleeping pills?)\b|\bnatural (means|doesn t mean|does not mean) safe\b
what: “Natural” doesn’t mean safe. Supplements aren’t checked like medicines before they are sold, and quality varies; a USP Verified or NSF mark means someone checked what is in the bottle.
Tell your pharmacist and doctor everything you take, and check with them before mixing anything with your medicines. Never mix sedating herbs with alcohol, sleeping pills, opioids or benzodiazepines.

what: The things with the best evidence are free: sleep, movement, slow breathing, less caffeine and alcohol, and talking to someone.

A few supplements, such as lavender oil capsules, lemon balm and L-theanine, have small, early studies, with small effects. Check with a pharmacist or doctor before trying any, especially alongside other medicines, and get help if anxiety is stopping your daily life.

how: Ask your doctor for a referral: they often know local counsellors, and what is covered.
Use a therapist directory you can filter by cost, place and focus, such as Psychology Today (US and UK) or the BACP directory (UK).
Through work: an Employee Assistance Program (EAP) often gives a few free, confidential sessions.

cards.name: after deployment: nightmares, being on edge
cards.pat: \bnightmares?\b.{0,50}\bon edge\b|\bon edge\b.{0,50}\bnightmares?\b|\bptsd\b|\bpost traumatic\b|\bjumps? at (every )?(noises?|sounds?|loud|bangs?)\b|\bhypervigilan\w*\b|\b(back|home) from (a |the |his |her |my )?(\w+ )?(deployment|tour|war|combat|service|the army|the navy)\b.{0,40}\b(normal|nightmares?|on edge|sleep|jumpy|angry|changed|different)\b|\b(since|after) (his |her |my |the )?(deployment|tour|combat)\b.{0,50}\b(nightmares?|on edge|sleep|jumpy|angry|changed|different|distant)\b|\b(veteran|military|army|navy|soldier|service member|marine)\b.{0,40}\b(nightmares?|on edge|cant sleep|doesnt sleep|jumpy)\b|\bnightmares? (since|after) (his |her |my |the )?(deployment|tour|combat|getting back|coming home)\b
what: Thank you for telling me. What you’re describing (nightmares, being on edge, jumping at noises, poor sleep) is common after deployment or anything frightening, and for many people it eases over the first weeks home. I can’t diagnose anyone, so I can’t say whether it’s PTSD. A doctor can, and there is good help for it.
how: See a doctor (or your unit’s medical team), especially if it lasts more than a month or gets in the way of sleep, work or home. Treatments for this work well.
In the US, Military OneSource is free and confidential, day or night: 800-342-9647. Veterans and service members can also dial 988 and then press 1 to talk to someone now.
In the UK, Combat Stress supports veterans and their families: 0800 138 1619.
At home: keep sleep and meals regular, go easy on alcohol, and agree a signal for “I need a few minutes” when it gets too much.
plain: This is common after deployment.
I cannot diagnose it.
Please see a doctor.
Military OneSource: 800-342-9647.
links: Sleep, nightmares and feeling on edge

cards.name: if you held the fort
what: That makes sense. You carried everything for months, and it’s normal to feel proud, tired and a little resentful all at once, and to find it hard when things change overnight. Resentment shows how much you carried. It isn’t a flaw.
how: Say it as a need, not a score.
Hand back the jobs you mind least first, not the ones you care about most.
Ask for a handover week before anything changes, and let some things be done differently.
Ask to be thanked if you need it. That’s a fair thing to want.
script: I’m so glad you’re home. I’m also tired, and some days I’m cross about how much I carried. It’s not about you. Can we talk about it on Sunday?
I got used to doing it my way while you were gone. Can we pick which jobs you take back?

cards.name: on edge and snapping after coming home
what: Feeling on edge and snapping more than you want to is very common after a deployment or anything very hard, and it isn’t a weakness. It’s worth taking seriously, for you and for the kids.
how: Make a pause plan while things are calm: a word that means “I need a break”, and a time you’ll come back.
When you feel it rising, step away, breathe out slower than you breathe in, then come back and repair.
Talk to your doctor about sleep and feeling on edge. Help works better when it starts early.
Support: in the US, Military OneSource is free and confidential, any time, on 800-342-9647 (veterans and service members can call 988, then press 1). In the UK, Combat Stress is on 0800 138 1619.
script: I snapped at you earlier. That wasn’t your fault. I’m still getting used to being home, and I’m sorry.

cards.name: sleep since coming home
what: Sleeping badly after coming home is very common, after a deployment or any time that was frightening or very hard. It’s not a weakness, and it’s worth raising with a doctor, because help tends to work better when it starts early.
how: Keep sleep and meals regular, and go easy on alcohol and late caffeine.
Slow breathing before bed helps many people: the Night Garden counts it for you.
See your doctor (or your unit’s medical team) if it lasts more than a few weeks, or comes with nightmares or feeling on edge.
Support: Military OneSource, 800-342-9647, free and confidential any time; in the UK, Combat Stress on 0800 138 1619.
script: You’ve been sleeping badly since you got back. Would you be willing to talk to a doctor about it? I’ll come with you if you want.

cards.name: coming home after time apart

what: Coming home after time apart is a big change for everyone: the one who was away, and the one who kept things running. Feeling like a stranger, or feeling stepped on, is very common in the first weeks, and it doesn’t mean anyone is failing.
how: Have a handover week: the one who held the fort shows how things run now, and the one coming back watches before changing anything.
Pick one or two jobs that are clearly the returning person’s, start to finish, so they have a real place, not leftover scraps.
Try changes as “let’s test it for two weeks”, not “the right way”.
Expect it to take weeks, not days. Check in once a week: what’s working, and what’s rubbing.
script: I’m so glad you’re home. The systems I built kept us going, and when they change overnight I feel wiped out. Can we do a handover week before we change things?
I want to be useful here, and I don’t know where I fit yet. Which jobs could be mine, start to finish?

what: Feeling like a stranger, or a guest, in your own house is very common in the first weeks back. You may come home to routines you don’t know, kids who have grown, and a partner who runs things smoothly without you. It usually eases as you find your jobs again.
how: Ask, don’t fix: ask which jobs your partner would like handed back, rather than changing how things are done.
Take whole jobs, start to finish, so you’re not “helping” on someone else’s job.
Leave their systems alone in week one. Rearranging the kitchen can land as “you did it wrong”.
Say thank you, specifically: name what they carried while you were away.
script: What would you like me to take back first? I’ll do it start to finish, your way for now.

what: You carried everything for months, and you got good at it. It’s normal to feel proud, tired and a little resentful all at once, and to find it hard when things you set up get changed.
how: Say the resentment as a need, not a score. It shows how much you carried; it isn’t a flaw.
Hand back the jobs you mind least first, not the ones you care about most.
Ask for a handover week: they watch before changing anything, and changes are a two-week test, not “the right way”.
Ask to be thanked if you need it. That’s a fair thing to want.

Say thank you, specifically: name the dog walks and the house.
Keep one fixed time together each week that isn’t about jobs.
script: Thank you for doing the dog and the house while I sleep. I see it. Could I take the shopping and the bins on my days off?

what: It can be, for a small number of people. The gaming guide’s line is: if gaming or a phone is crowding out sleep, work, money or friends, and cutting back is hard even when you want to, that’s worth talking about with a doctor. It isn’t a character flaw, and help is there. For most couples, though, it’s about timing, not the hours.
how: Check the four: sleep, work or school, money, friends. Is any of them being crowded out?
Ask yourself honestly whether cutting back is hard even when you want to.
If neither fits, it’s probably a timing problem: agree when game time is, and when time together is.
Before deciding whether she’s overreacting, ask what she’s worried about, and say it back.
script: I don’t think I’m addicted, but I hear that you’re worried. Can we look at when I play, and pick evenings that are ours?

cards.name: raising gaming without a fight
what: Talks about gaming go wrong mostly because of timing. Raise it mid-match and it sounds like an attack while they can’t stop; wait until you’re fed up and it comes out as “You’re always on that thing.”
how: Pick a set time when you’re both calm, not the moment you’ve had enough.
Start by saying back what the game gives them: friends, a way to switch off, being good at something.
Make one clear ask with a day and a time, not “more time together”.
If it gets heated, stop and come back to it. A short pause beats a fight about a game.
script: Can we talk about the weekend tonight after dinner? It’s nothing bad.
So the game is where you see your friends, and it helps you switch off after work. Did I get that? I’d love Thursday evenings to be ours.

cards.name: guilt about a quiet friendship
what: Feeling guilty shows how much the friendship matters to you. The trouble is that guilt makes replying feel bigger, so the gap grows. A short, honest message now is kinder than a perfect one later.
how: Send something short today. Ten seconds is enough.
Say why in a few words, so they don’t think it’s about them.
Thank them for still reaching out.
script: I’ve been underwater with the baby. I miss you and I’m not ignoring you. Voice note this weekend?
Thank you for always being the one who reaches out. I notice, even when I’m slow to reply.

cards.name: stopping texting a friend to see if they notice
what: You can step back, and it’s okay to protect your energy. Going silent to see if she notices usually turns into a stand-off where you both wait. Saying it once, kindly, and then giving her room tends to work better.
how: Say it once, as a feeling and a small ask, not a test.
Then give it a few days, and let her come towards you for a while.
If nothing changes over months, you can let the friendship be lighter for now. That isn’t failing.
script: I’ve noticed I’m usually the one who plans. I don’t mind, I’d just love to hear from you first sometimes.

cards.notPat: \b(died|passed|funeral|dead|killed|cancer|hospital|cuts? (herself|himself|themselves)|hurt\w* (herself|himself|themselves)|help plan|plan anything|plans? (things|stuff|trips?|nights? out)|friend group|group chat|split (the )?(bill|costs?)|pay (their|her|his) share)\b
what: Friendships drift most when life changes: a new baby, a move, a new job, or just low energy. It rarely means the friendship is over. It usually needs a smaller, kinder rhythm for a while.
how: Send something that needs no reply: “Thinking of you. No need to answer.”
If you’re the one with no energy, say so plainly. Silence can read as not caring; one honest line doesn’t.
If you’re always the one reaching out, say it once, kindly, then let them come towards you for a while.
Suggest something easy: a walk with the pram, a ten-minute call, a voice note.
script: I still care about you so much. I’m low on energy and slow to reply right now, and it’s not about you.
I miss you. I know life is full right now. No need to reply, I just wanted you to know I’m thinking of you.
scriptLabels: A text you could send now

sides.re: \b(i m|im|i am|i ve been|ive been|i have been) (neglecting|ignoring|bad at (replying|texting)|slow to reply|not replying|too tired)\b|\bneglect\w* (my )?(best |old |close )?friend|\b(i have|i ve got|ive got|i just had) (a )?(newborn|new baby|baby)\b|\bi (never|dont|don t|cant|can t) (reply|text back|answer)\b|\bi have no energy\b|\bno energy to reply\b
what: Some seasons take everything you have. A new baby, a new job, an illness: going quiet then is very common, and it doesn’t mean you don’t care. The guilt can make replying feel even harder, so the gap grows. Your friend doesn’t need a long catch-up, just to know they still matter.
how: Send something short today. Ten seconds is enough: a small message now beats a perfect one next month.
Say why, in a few words, so they don’t fill the silence with “it’s me”.
Offer one easy next thing: a voice note, a call while you walk, or them coming over while you’re in pajamas.
Thank them for reaching out. They’ve been holding the thread for both of you.
script: I’ve been underwater with the baby. I miss you and I’m not ignoring you. Voice note this weekend?
I still care about you so much. I’m low on energy and slow to reply right now, and it’s not about you.
scriptLabels: A text you could send now
links: If you’re the one who went quiet

sides.re: \b(never|doesnt|doesn t|dont|don t|stopped|hardly|barely|no longer|rarely) (texts?|replies|reply|replying|answers?|calls?|reaches? out|messages?|gets? in touch)\b|\b(i m|im|i am) always (the one|reaching out|texting first)\b|\bi (always )?(text|message|reach out|plan) first\b|\bi m the only one\b|\bwaiting (for|on) (her|him|them)\b
what: It hurts to feel like the only one holding a friendship up, and that feeling is worth saying out loud. It’s rarely the whole story, though: a new baby, a new job or low energy usually explains the quiet, not how much they care about you.
how: Check what’s going on for them. Going quiet is usually about how much someone has left, not about you.
Say it once, as a feeling and a small ask, not a list of every time you texted first.
Make the ask tiny: ten minutes, a voice note, a walk with the pram. Easy to say yes to.
Then give it a few days. One kind message works better than three.
script: I miss you and I’ve been feeling a bit left out. Could we find ten minutes this week?
I know life is full right now. No pressure to reply properly. I’d love a voice note when you can.

cards.notPat: \b(kids?|children|stepkids?|step ?(son|daughter|children|child)|his son|her son|his daughter|her daughter|my own|every other weekend|weekends? with us)\b
what: Moving into a home that already has its own rhythm often leaves the newest person feeling like a guest for a while. That’s about how the home runs, not about whether you’re wanted.
how: Ask for one or two jobs and one space that are clearly yours, so you’re part of how things run.
Ask to be in on house decisions from now on, at a set time each week, with everyone.
Change one small thing so it feels like your home too: a shelf, a meal, where something lives.
Say how it feels, without blame: “I love being here, and I still feel like a guest.”
script: I love living with you, and I still feel like a guest. Could I take over the groceries and have a say in house decisions, so it feels like my home too?

what: Yes. Every tool here works for two to eight partners, and nothing here assumes there are only two of you. Where a page says “partner”, read it as “each partner”.
how: The Lemonade Stand and One owner per job take up to eight names: each person fills in their own side on their own phone, and you merge them.
Watch for one person becoming the hub who plans and merges everything. Rotate who runs the monthly look-back.
Someone newer to the home often feels like a guest: give them clear jobs and a real say, not just a room.
Check-ins work for three too: each person gets a turn, and each pair can have its own time as well.

cards.name: being left out of household decisions
cards.pat: \b(left out of|not included in|out of the loop (on|about|with)|no say in|dont get a say in|never get a say in|not part of) (the |our |house |household |family |big )?(decisions?|plans?|planning|what happens|choices)\b|\b(decisions?|plans?|choices) (get|are|were|got) made without me\b|\b(decide|decides|decided|deciding) (everything|things) without me\b|\b(how do i|how can i|i want to|how to) (get|have) (a|more of a) say\b(?=.{4,})
what: Being out of the loop at home hurts, and long hours make it easy to happen without anyone meaning it. A small routine usually fixes it better than one big talk.
how: Agree a short weekly decisions slot (15 minutes, same time each week) where anything that affects everyone gets decided.
Keep a shared “to decide” list in between, so things wait for the slot instead of being settled in passing.
Agree what anyone can decide alone (small, everyday things) and what needs everyone (money over an agreed amount, plans, guests).
If you can’t make the slot, send your view in writing beforehand, and it counts.
script: I know I’m not around much with my hours, and I still want a say. Could we keep a 15-minute decisions slot on Sundays, and a list for things that can wait till then?

cards.name: a teen in foster or kinship care
cards.pat: \b(i m|im|i am|i ve been|ive been|i have been|i live|i m living|im living|i got put|i was put) (in|into|with) (foster care|care|a foster (family|home|carer|placement)|my foster (carers?|family|mum|mom|dad|parents)|a placement)\b|\bmy (foster )?(carers|foster (carers?|mum|mom|dad|parents|family|home))\b.{0,50}\b(rules?|strict|dont get|don t get|do not get|wont let|won t let|took|take|hate|unfair|annoying|shout\w*|treat)\b|\b(hate|hating) (the|their|all the) rules\b.{0,30}\b(foster|placement|carers?)\b|\bmy (social worker|placement)\b.{0,40}\b(rules?|move|moving|family|mum|mom|dad|school|friends|hate)\b
what: That sounds hard. A new home often means new rules all at once, and it’s normal to feel on guard, or angry, for a while. You don’t have to settle in fast, or pretend it’s fine.
how: Ask for the reason behind one rule, at a calm moment, then suggest a deal: “10 on school nights, 11 on weekends?”
You can say what you miss. Missing your old home or your family isn’t ungrateful.
You can ask your social worker, or an advocate, about things you want to change: seeing your family, keeping your old school or friends, or a house rule. You’re allowed to ask, and to ask again.
If you want to talk to someone outside the house, Childline (UK) is free on 0800 1111, any time.
script: I know you’re doing a lot for me. Can we talk about the phone rule? I’ve got an idea.
I’m not angry at you. I’m just missing home today.

cards.name: two carers, firm and warm
cards.pat: \bfoster\w*\b.{0,80}\b(stricter|too strict|too soft|firmer|softer|disagree about (rules|discipline))\b|\b(stricter|too soft|firmer)\b.{0,80}\bfoster\w*\b
what: It’s very common for one carer to be firmer and the other warmer. Both are care: one wants safety and predictability, the other wants the child to feel heard. The trouble starts when the child hears two different rulebooks.
how: On a calm evening, without the child, each of you writes your top three non-negotiable rules. Only three.
Compare. Keep the ones you share, and agree which ones the child will hear.
Agree who holds each rule: one of you leads on bedtime, the other on homework, and the other backs them up.
Disagree in private. In front of the child, you’re on the same side. Look again in two weeks.
script: I worry she’ll feel unsafe without clear limits. Can we pick three rules we both hold?
I’ll back you up on the phone rule. Can you take the lead on it?

cards.name: the paperwork side of foster and kinship care
cards.pat: \bfoster\w*\b.{0,80}\b(meetings|paperwork|appointments|reviews|forms|contact visits)\b|\b(meetings|paperwork|appointments|reviews|forms|contact visits)\b.{0,80}\bfoster\w*\b|\b(emotional|feelings) (work|stuff|load|labou?r|side)\b.{0,40}\bfoster\w*\b|\bfoster\w*\b.{0,60}\b(emotional|feelings) (work|stuff|load|labou?r|side)\b
what: Foster and kinship care comes with a second, hidden job: social worker visits, reviews and meetings, the daily log, contact arrangements, and the feelings work of being there after a hard day. When one of you carries most of it, it wears you out, and it’s worth sharing on purpose.
how: Write every job down for one month, the feelings work included: meetings, the log, calls, contact visits, the talk after a hard day.
Give each job one owner. A weekly meeting is heavier than one school email, so look at the weight, not just the number.
Take turns going to reviews, or go together, so you both know the plan.
Agree the rules in private, so the child hears one plan. If one of you is firmer and the other warmer, pick three rules you both hold.
script: Could you take the evening calls and one meeting a month? I’ll keep the daily log.
I’m doing most of the emotional side after contact. Could you take the bedtime talk two nights a week?

cards.name: a consequence that isn’t landing
cards.pat: \b(laughs?|laughing|laughed|shrugs?|smirks?|doesnt care|dont care|does not care|couldnt care less)\b.{0,30}\b(when|if) (i|we) (take|took|confiscate\w*|ground\w*|say no|punish\w*|tell (her|him|them) off|remove)\b|\b(consequences?|punishments?|taking (her|his|their) phone( away)?|grounding)\b.{0,30}\b(dont|doesnt|don t|never|not|isnt|aren t|arent) (work|working|matter|bother|landing)\b
what: When a consequence gets a laugh, it usually isn’t landing, and a bigger one rarely fixes that. Laughing can be a young person’s way of saying “you can’t get to me”, especially if they’ve had a lot of adults come and go.
how: Stay calm and don’t argue about the laugh. Say what happens, once, and then do it.
Tie the consequence to the rule and its reason: phone downstairs at 10, because sleep makes everything easier. Give it back at the time you said.
Keep connection separate from consequences: one small daily moment with them that they can’t lose.
Agree the rules with any other carer first, so they hear one plan, and look again in two weeks. If they’re in care, your social worker can help with a plan that fits their history.
script: I’m not going to argue about it. The phone stays downstairs tonight, and you’ll have it back at 7 tomorrow. I still want to hear about your day.

what: A teen who pushes every limit is often checking whether the limits hold, and whether you’ll stay calm. A few rules with a reason, kept calmly every time, usually work better than bigger punishments.
how: Say the why with the rule: “Tell us where you’re going and when you’ll be back, because we worry, not because we don’t trust you.”
Write the rules down together, and let them suggest changes: “11 on weekends, 10 on school nights?” Rules they helped make are easier to keep.
Agree one calm consequence in advance, and keep it the same every time. Keep one small daily moment of connection they can’t lose.
If there are two of you, hold the same three rules, and disagree in private.
script: We’re not trying to control you. We worry when we don’t know where you are. Can we agree a time together, and you text if you’ll be late?
Phones downstairs at 10 on school nights, because sleep makes everything easier. What time would you suggest at weekends?

cards.name: fostering and adoption: a child who pushes you away
cards.pat: \bfoster\w*\b|\bkinship (care|carers?|family|families)\b|\bspecial guardian\w*\b|\b(our|my) (adopted|adoptive) (son|daughter|child|kid|kids|children)\b|\b(moved|been moved|moves) (homes|houses|placements|around|schools) (a lot|so much|so many times|many times)\b|\b(she|he|they) (has|have|s) (been in|had) (lots of|so many|many) (homes|placements)\b
what: Children who have moved homes a lot often push away the people trying hardest, because getting close has felt risky before. It usually isn’t about you, and it isn’t a sign you’re failing.
how: Aim for predictable, not perfect: the same routines, the same goodnight, the same “see you after school” every day.
Keep connection separate from behaviour: one small daily moment with her that she can’t lose for bad behaviour.
Name it without pressure: “You don’t have to trust us yet. We’re not going anywhere.”
Get support for you too: your social worker, a carers’ support group, and training on trauma and attachment.
script: You don’t have to trust us yet. We’re staying, and we’ll keep showing up.

cards.pat: \bseen and not heard\b|\b(i was|we were) (brought up|raised|taught)\b.{0,50}\b(am i (doing it )?wrong|doing it wrong|old fashioned|too strict)\b|\b(things|parenting|it) (was|were) different (when i was|in my day)\b.{0,40}\b(wrong|grandchild|grandkids|grandson|granddaughter)\b|\b(my )?(daughter|son|kids|children)\b.{0,25}\b(says|thinks|tells me)\b.{0,10}\b(i m|im|i am) (too )?(strict|old fashioned|harsh)\b.{0,40}\b(grandchild\w*|grandkids?|grandson|granddaughter|brought up|raised|my day)?
what: No, not wrong. You were raised by the rules of your time, and your grown child is raising theirs by the rules of now. Neither is wrong: they’re two rulebooks from two different times. Small changes go a long way, and you don’t have to change who you are.
how: Ask the parents for their top three rules, and keep to those. Everything else can be your own way.
Their house, their rules; your house, a few gentle ones you agree on.
Keep the respect and kindness you were raised with, and add one new habit: ask “How was your day?” and listen to the whole answer.
When you hear “you’re too strict”, ask what the one thing is, rather than defend: “What would you like me to do differently? I’m happy to change it.”
script: I was brought up differently, and I’m still learning. Tell me how you’d like me to handle it, and I’ll try.

cards.name: disagreeing about how strict to be
cards.pat: \b(we|my (wife|husband|partner)|she|he|they)\b.{0,30}\b(disagree|argue|fight|clash|row)\w*\b.{0,30}\b(how strict|strict|discipline|rules|parenting|consequences|bedtime|screen time)\b|\b(thinks|says|feels) (i m|im|i am) (too|so) (strict|soft|lenient|harsh|easy)\b|\b(too strict|too soft|too lenient)\b.{0,20}\b(with|on) (the |our |my )?(kids?|children|son|daughter|her|him)\b|\bdisagree (about|on) parenting\b|\bhow strict (to be|should (we|i) be)\b
what: Most parents disagree about how strict to be, and it usually comes from how each of you was raised. Children do best when the adults back a few rules together, not when both parents are exactly the same.
how: Talk away from the children: each of you says why it matters to you, and what you’re worried about.
Agree three to five house rules you both back, and what happens if one is broken.
Outside those, allow different styles: one of you can be softer on some things.
Don’t overrule each other in front of the children. Talk about it later, in private.
script: I know I come across as strict. I worry about her. Can we agree a few rules we both back, and let the rest be flexible?

what: A few clear rules work better than many. Here are rules many families use for a 13 to 16 year old. Pick the ones that fit, and agree them with your teen if you can: rules they helped make are easier to keep.
how: Phones charge outside the bedroom at night (say from 9:30 on school nights).
Say where you’re going and who with, and text if plans change.
Home by an agreed time, which moves later as trust grows.
One or two jobs that are yours, like your own laundry and the dishes twice a week.
We can disagree without insults, and that goes for the adults too.

cards.name: raising a grandchild
cards.pat: \b(raising|bringing up|looking after|caring for|have custody of|got custody of) (my|our) (grandson|granddaughter|grandchild\w*|grandkids?|niece|nephew|grandbaby)\b|\b(grandparent|grandma|grandmother|grandad|granddad|grandpa|grandfather|nan|nana|granny)s?\b.{0,40}\b(raising|bringing up|full time|custody|guardian\w*)\b|\b(raising|bringing up|full time|custody of)\b.{0,40}\b(grandparent|grandson|granddaughter|grandchild\w*|grandkids?)\b|\b(i m|im|i am) raising (him|her|them) (full time|on my own|myself|now)\b|\bkinship\b
what: Raising a grandchild is a huge act of love, and it’s exhausting, often on top of worry and grief about their parent. You don’t have to do it alone, and there is help for exactly this.
how: Look for kinship carer support: in the UK, the charity Kinship (kinship.org.uk) gives free advice; in the US, search “grandfamilies” or your state’s kinship navigator program.
Ask about money and legal help: you may be entitled to support, and a guardianship or custody order can make school and doctors easier.
Keep routines simple and predictable. Children who have been through upheaval settle with sameness.
Tell him what’s happening in words he can manage, and look after your own rest: one real break a week is part of caring for him.
script: Mum is getting help to get well. You’re living with me now, and I’m not going anywhere.

cards.name: when a parent misses a visit

what: Waiting for a parent who doesn’t come can bring up love, hope, anger and disappointment all at once. You don’t need perfect words. Plain and kind is enough.
how: If a visit is cancelled, say it plainly and kindly, and don’t promise the next one will happen.
Keep that evening light: a favourite meal, a film, no big talks and no new rules.
Never criticise his parent, even when you’re upset about what happened. He may hear it as criticism of him.
Don’t ask for a full report. Let him tell you if and when he wants to.

Visits can bring up a lot. You don’t have to talk about it. I’m around if you want to.
plain: Say it plainly and kindly.
Don’t promise the next visit.
Keep the evening light.
Never criticise their parent.

cards.name: a teen who feels the adult at home doesn’t get them
cards.pat: \b(nan|nana|nanna|gran|granny|grandma|grandmother|grandad|granddad|grandpa|grandfather|grandparents?|carers?|foster (carers?|mum|mom|dad|parents?)|aunt|auntie|uncle)\b.{0,40}\b(doesnt|don t|dont|does not|do not|never|wont|won t) (get|understand|listen to|hear) me\b
what: Feeling like the person you live with doesn’t get you is lonely, even when they’re trying. It’s really common across two generations, and it isn’t your fault.
how: Pick one thing you wish she understood, and say just that one thing, at a calm moment.
Ask what she worries about, too. A rule is often a worry in disguise.
Find one other adult who does get you (a teacher, a school counsellor, an aunt) and talk to them as well.
If things at home are more than clashing, Childline (UK) is free on 0800 1111, any time.
script: Can I tell you one thing I wish you got about me? I’m not having a go.
links: For teens: living with grandparents, family or foster carers

cards.name: house rules with the adults you live with (for teens)
cards.pat: \b(nan|nana|nanna|gran|granny|grandma|grandmother|grandad|granddad|grandpa|grandfather|grandparents?|carers?|foster (carers?|mum|mom|dad|parents?|family)|aunt|auntie|uncle|mum|mom|dad|mother|father|parents?|stepmum|stepmom|stepdad)\b.{0,30}\b(takes?|took|taking|keeps taking|confiscat\w*) (away )?my (phone|tablet|ipad|laptop|switch|xbox|playstation|ps5|console)\b|\b(nan|nana|nanna|gran|granny|grandma|grandmother|grandad|granddad|grandpa|grandfather|grandparents?|carers?|foster (carers?|mum|mom|dad|parents?|family)|aunt|auntie|uncle)\b.{0,40}\b((so|too|really|very|super) strict|is strict|s strict|doesn t get me|doesnt get me|does not get me|don t get me|dont get me|doesn t understand me|doesnt understand me|old ?fashioned|too many rules|curfew|won t let me|wont let me|nags? me|nagging me)\b|\b(i m|im|i am) 1[0-7]\b.{0,60}\b(nan|nana|nanna|gran|granny|grandma|grandmother|grandad|granddad|grandpa|grandfather|grandparents?|carers?|foster (carers?|mum|mom|dad|parents?|family)|aunt|auntie|uncle|mum|mom|dad|mother|father|parents?|stepmum|stepmom|stepdad)\b.{0,40}\b(strict|doesn t get me|doesnt get me|don t get me|dont get me|old ?fashioned|too many rules|curfew|won t let me|wont let me)\b
what: That sounds frustrating. Clashing over rules with the adult you live with is really common, especially across two generations. It doesn’t mean either of you is doing it wrong, and it usually goes better as a deal than a fight.
how: Ask for the reason behind the rule, calmly and at a good moment, not right after a row. There’s usually a worry underneath: sleep, school, or who you’re talking to.
Then suggest a deal that covers their worry: “10 on school nights, 11 at weekends?” or “The phone charges in the kitchen, and I get it back after homework.”
Say what you need too: “Messaging my friends after school is how we keep in touch.”
If they still say no, ask when you can try again, like in a month. Keeping a deal for a few weeks is the quickest way to more freedom.

If someone at home scares you, hurts you or cuts you off from everyone, that’s different, and it isn’t your fault. Tell a trusted adult, or call Childline free on 0800 1111 (UK) or Childhelp on 1-800-422-4453 (US).
script: I know you’re doing a lot for me. Can we talk about the phone rule? I’ve got an idea: 10 on school nights, 11 at weekends?

cards.name: when a parent is away (for young people)
cards.pat: \b(i m|im|i am) 1[0-7]\b.{0,40}\b(live|living|stay|staying) with (my )?(grandma|grandmother|nan|nana|granny|grandad|grandpa|grandparents|aunt|auntie|uncle|foster \w+)\b|\b(my )?(mum|mom|dad|mother|father|parents?) (is|are|s|has gone|went) (in|into|to) (rehab|prison|jail|treatment|recovery)\b
what: That’s a lot to carry. When a parent is away, in rehab, or not able to look after you, it’s normal to feel worried, angry, sad or even relieved, sometimes all at once. None of it is your fault.
how: You’re allowed to ask questions about what’s happening, and to say when you don’t want to talk about it.
Pick one adult you trust (your grandparent, a teacher, a school counsellor) and tell them how you’re really doing.
If you want to talk to someone outside the family: in the UK, Childline is free on 0800 1111; in the US, you can text HOME to 741741.
It’s okay to love your parent and still be upset with them.
links: For teens: when a parent is away

cards.name: missing a parent who is away
what: Missing your mum makes sense, even when things are complicated. It’s okay to love her and still be upset with her, and it isn’t your fault that she’s away.
how: All of it is allowed: missing her, being angry with her, feeling relieved, or all three in one day.
You choose who knows. One friend or one adult is enough.
Tell the adult you live with when it’s a missing-her day. It helps them not take it personally.
Free people to talk to: Childline (UK) 0800 1111, any time. If a parent drinks, Nacoa (UK) and Alateen (US) are there for you.
script: I’m not angry at you. I’m just missing Mum today.
Can we talk about Mum? I keep thinking about her.

cards.name: missing someone
cards.pat: ^(i )?(really |so |just |still )?miss (my|our) (mum|mom|mother|dad|father|parents?|grandma|grandmother|nan|nana|grandad|grandpa|brother|sister|son|daughter|kids|children|wife|husband|partner|boyfriend|girlfriend|friend|best friend|family|home|old life)( so much| a lot| loads)?$|^i (really |so |just |still )?miss (him|her|them)( so much| a lot)?$
what: Missing someone hurts because they matter to you. That ache is love with nowhere to go for a while.
how: If you can reach them, tell them: a short message, a voice note, or a call.
If you can’t, it can help to write to them anyway, or to talk about them with someone who knows them.
Keep one small thing that connects you: a photo, a song, a ritual.
If missing them comes with worry (they’re ill, away or in treatment), tell someone you trust how you’re doing.

cards.name: a child or teen on their phone at night
cards.pat: \b(my|our) (son|daughter|grandson|granddaughter|kid|kids|teen\w*|child|children|1[0-9] ?year ?old)\b.{0,40}\b(phone|screen|tablet|ipad|games?|gaming)\b.{0,40}\b(all night|late|in bed|bedtime|sleep|night)\b
what: Phones at night are one of the most common battles with children and teens, and sleep is worth protecting. A clear, calm house rule usually works better than nightly arguments.
how: Agree a phone bedtime: phones charge outside the bedroom, say from 9:30 on school nights.
Explain the why (sleep, mood, school), not just the rule.
Make it a house rule for everyone, adults too if you can.
Use the phone’s built-in controls or a wifi schedule as backup, not instead of the talk.
script: Phones sleep in the kitchen from 9:30. It’s not a punishment. Sleep matters for all of us.
links: For teens: the other side of house rules

cards.name: a child with ADHD who forgets
what: Forgetting is one of the most frustrating parts, for everyone. It usually isn’t laziness or not caring: their short-term memory drops things more easily, so put the memory outside their head.
how: Write it down where they’ll see it: a list on the fridge, a picture checklist by the door.
Same place, every time: shoes, bag and coat live in one spot.
Remind without the sigh. A calm reminder works better than “How many times…?”
script: I’ll write it on the fridge so we both remember.
Check your door list: shoes, bag, lunch. What’s missing?

cards.name: a child with ADHD who can’t sit still
what: Moving often helps a child with ADHD think. Telling them to “sit still” can use up all their focus on keeping still, with nothing left for the task.
how: Build in movement: a short break every 10 to 15 minutes, or a job that means walking.
Give their hands something to do: a squishy toy, a bit of modelling clay.
Pick your battles. Wriggling at the table is fine. Running in the road is not.
script: Let’s take a wiggle break, then back to it.
You can hold the squishy ball while we read. Your hands can move, your ears listen.

cards.name: what to say to a child with ADHD
what: You’re probably not saying anything wrong. With ADHD, how you say it matters more than the exact words: one thing at a time, and lots of noticing what goes right.
how: Get their attention first: say their name, get close, wait for their eyes.
Give one short instruction, then ask them to say it back: “What are you off to do?”
Praise the effort, specifically: “You remembered your bag all by yourself.”
Ask the parents what works at home, and do the same at yours.
script: I saw you stop and think before you answered. That was hard, and you did it.

cards.name: when a child has ADHD
cards.pat: \b(my|our|his|her|their) (son|daughter|kid|kids|child|children|grandson|granddaughter|grandchild\w*|grandkids?|stepson|stepdaughter|boy|girl|little one|nephew|niece|pupil|student)\b.{0,40}\b(adhd|add|attention deficit)\b|\b(adhd|add)\b.{0,30}\b(in )?(children|kids|child|boys|girls|toddlers?)\b|\bis adhd (real|made up|an excuse|just|a real)\b|\badhd\b.{0,20}\b(or|vs|versus|just) (just )?(bad|naughty|poor)? ?(behaviou?r|parenting|upbringing|discipline)\b|\b(what is|explain) adhd\b|\b(he|she|my (son|daughter|grandson|granddaughter|kid|child|boy|girl)) (can t|cant|cannot|won t|wont) (sit still|stay still|stop fidgeting)\b
what: Yes, ADHD is real and well studied. It is not bad behaviour or bad upbringing. In plain words: a child with ADHD has a brain that finds it harder to keep attention on dull things, to wait, to sit still and to remember steps, even when they really want to.
how: Talk in short, single steps, and get eye contact first: “Shoes on, then come back to me.”
Expect forgetting, and use reminders that don’t nag: a picture list by the door, a timer, one step at a time.
Give movement on purpose when he can’t sit still: let him stand, fidget or squeeze something while he listens.
Catch him doing well and say so, often. Many children with ADHD hear “no” all day.
Agree two or three rules with the parents that you all keep, so he hears the same thing in every home.
script: I can see sitting still is hard right now. Want to stand up and help me stir, and tell me about it while we cook?
One thing at a time: shoes first. Then come and tell me, and we’ll do the next bit.
plain: ADHD is real. It is not bad behaviour or bad parenting.
The brain finds it harder to focus on dull things, to wait, to sit still and to remember steps.
Use short, single steps.
Let them move while they listen.
Praise often.

cards.name: a parent who turns up and judges
cards.pat: \b(she|he|they|my (mum|mom|mother|dad|father|parents|mil|mother in law|motherinlaw|in laws|inlaws))\b.{0,30}\b(turns? up|shows? up|drops? (in|by|round)|comes? (round|over))\b.{0,40}\b(no warning|without (warning|calling|asking|texting|ringing)|unannounced|uninvited)\b.{0,60}\b(wrong|criticis\w*|criticiz\w*|judg\w*|comments?|advice|tells me (how|what)|lectur\w*)\b
what: That sounds draining: a visit you didn’t expect, and then feeling judged in your own home. You’re allowed to ask for both to change, kindly.
how: Ask for a heads-up: a text before coming over, or a regular visiting time.
For the advice, one line is enough: “Thanks, I know you mean well. I’ll ask when I want a tip.”
Say it once, kindly, then follow through. If they turn up anyway, it’s okay to say today isn’t a good day.
Now and then, ask for their advice on something you’d genuinely value. It makes the “not this time” easier to hear.
script: I love seeing you. Could you text before coming over, so I can make sure it’s a good time?
Thanks, I know you mean well. We’re going to try it our way for now.

cards.name: a grandparent’s help that isn’t wanted
cards.pat: \b(my )?(daughter|son|daughterinlaw|soninlaw|daughter in law|son in law|kids|children)\b.{0,30}\b(doesnt|does not|dont|wont|will not|never)\b.{0,10}\b(want|like|take|listen to|ask for)\b.{0,15}\b(my )?(advice|help|opinion|input|ideas)\b|\b(turn|turning|show|showing|come|coming|pop|popping|drop|dropping) (up|round|over|by|in) (unannounced|without (calling|asking|warning|texting|ringing))\b|\bi (just )?(turn|show|pop) up\b|\bi (only|just) want(ed)? to help\b
what: Wanting to help is love. It’s also normal for new parents to want to find their own way, and to need to plan around naps and sleep. What usually works best is asking before advising, and calling before visiting.
how: Ask first: “Would you like my thoughts, or would you rather I just listen?” Then go with the answer.
Text before you visit, and let them pick the time. It isn’t a rule against you.
Offer help that’s easy to say yes to: a meal, a load of washing, an hour with the baby so they can sleep.
If you feel hurt, say it once, gently, then let it rest.
script: I’d love to help in whatever way suits you. Would you like my thoughts on things, or would you rather I just listen for now?

cards.name: what to text back when you’re hurt
what: It makes sense to feel hurt. You can answer kindly without pretending it didn’t sting, and a short reply usually lands best.
how: Wait until the first sting passes. A reply in an hour beats one in a minute.
Say the feeling in one line, without blame.
Then say yes to what they asked, and one thing you’d love: a regular time, a photo, a call.
Check it in the Chat analyzer before you send, if you like.

cards.name: feeling shut out from a grandchild
cards.pat: \b(shut|pushed|kept|cut) out (of|from) (my )?(grandchild\w*|grandkids?|grandson|granddaughter|grandbaby|the baby|their lives|the kids lives)\b|\b(dont|do not|never|cant|not allowed to|wont let me) (get to )?see (my )?(grandchild\w*|grandkids?|grandson|granddaughter|grandbaby)\b|\b(miss|missing) (my )?(grandchild\w*|grandkids?|grandson|granddaughter|grandbaby)\b
what: I’m sorry. Feeling shut out from a grandchild you love really hurts, and that hurt deserves to be named before anything else.
how: Give the hurt somewhere to go first: talk to a friend, or write it down, before you talk to the parents.
Ask the parents, not the child, what would help: “I miss our time together. Is there a way I could see them that works for you?”
Keep to their rules for now, even if you’d do it differently. Trust comes back by keeping them.
Stay in touch in small ways they’re comfortable with: a card, a short video, a regular call.
script: I miss them, and I miss you. Is there a way I could see them that works for you?

cards.name: a parent who feels kept from the baby
what: It’s common for a parent to feel left out when a baby arrives, and to say it as hurt. Her being upset doesn’t mean your boundary was wrong. Giving her a real role, and saying why, usually helps more than backing down.
how: Acknowledge the feeling first: “I can hear how much you want to be close to her.”
Name your top three baby rules. Everything else can be her way.
Give her a real role: bath time on Tuesdays, a walk with the pram, a meal dropped off.
Write a short family plan together, and look at it again in two weeks.
script: I’m not keeping her from you. I love that you want to be close. Could you do Tuesday bath time? That would really help us.
These are our three rules for the baby. Everything else, do it your way.

what: A short plan, written together, takes the guessing out of visits and advice. Keep it small.
how: Visits: text first, and a regular time, like Sunday afternoon and one weekday.
Advice: ask first: “Would you like a tip, or just a listening ear?”
The baby: your top three rules, and a regular job for Grandma or Grandad.
Review: twenty minutes together in two weeks. What’s working? What needs a change?

cards.name: a parent who is homophobic about your partner
cards.pat: \b(homophob\w*|transphob\w*|biphob\w*|anti gay|nasty|rude|horrible|mean|awful)\b.{0,40}\b(about|to) (my )?(girlfriend|boyfriend|partner|wife|husband|gf|bf)\b|\b(dad|mum|mom|father|mother|parents?|family|brother|sister)\b.{0,40}\b(homophob\w*|transphob\w*|biphob\w*)\b
what: You can love them and still hold a line. Hearing that about someone you love hurts, and you don’t have to sit through it.
how: Decide before the next visit what you’ll do if it happens: say your line once, calmly, and leave if it carries on.
Keep your partner out of the crossfire. Talk to your parent yourself, one to one. It isn’t your partner’s job to win them over.
Leave the door open on your terms: shorter visits, with a set end time and a leaving line you agree beforehand.
If you rely on them for a home or money, plan your safety first.
script: I want you in my life, and I need you to treat [her name] with respect. If that can’t happen today, I’ll head home, and I’ll call you next week.

cards.name: setting a kind boundary with family
cards.pat: \b(set|setting|draw|hold|keep|have)\b.{0,15}\bboundar\w*\b.{0,40}\b(mum|mom|mother|dad|father|parents?|mil|motherinlaw|mother in law|inlaws|in laws|family|sister|brother|nan|grandma)\b|\bboundar\w*\b.{0,30}\bwith (my )?(mum|mom|mother|dad|father|parents?|mil|motherinlaw|mother in law|inlaws|in laws|family|sister|brother|nan|grandma)\b|\bset (a |some )?boundar\w* (kindly|without hurting|gently|nicely)\b|\bboundar\w*\b.{0,30}\bwithout hurting\b|\b(tell|ask|get)\b.{0,10}\b(my )?(mum|mom|mother|dad|father|parents?|mil|motherinlaw|mother in law|inlaws|in laws|nan|grandma)\b.{0,25}\b(text|call|ring|phone|check|ask)\w*\b.{0,15}\b(before|first)\b.{0,20}\b(visit\w*|coming|comes|come over|dropping by|drops by|turning up|turns up)\b
what: You can love someone and still say no to some things. A kind boundary is about what you will do, said warmly, not a rule for them.
how: Pick the one thing that matters most, not everything at once.
Say it with love first, then the limit, then what you can offer: “I love seeing you. Please call before you come. Sunday afternoons are great.”
Expect a little hurt or pushback. That doesn’t mean you were unkind. Say it again, calmly.
Back it up with actions: if she drops in anyway, “It’s not a good time. Let’s do Sunday.”
script: I love you, and I want us to stay close. I need to make some decisions myself, and I’ll ask when I want advice.

what: Lateness at pick-up is worth raising, for your child’s sake: waiting at the door is hard on a kid. Keep it to one clear, firm ask about the time, not a verdict on the other parent. Firm and friendly can go together.
how: Say it once, in writing, about the child: the time, and what you need. A plain statement is fine; it doesn’t have to be a question. Never at the door in front of your child.
Talk about your child’s needs, not the other parent’s character: “She waited forty minutes” lands; “You’re always late” starts a war.
Keep it Brief, Informative, Friendly and Firm, as many family professionals suggest. Answer only the question asked, and skip the history.
If nothing changes, send one reminder with a date, then do what you said, calmly, and keep the message thread as your record.

cards.name: getting a say as a co-parent
what: You can ask for a say without starting a fight. What usually works is agreeing once, in writing, which decisions are joint, and how you ask each other.
how: Name the joint decisions: usually school, health and anything new and regular, like a club, a sport or a camp. Day-to-day things belong to whoever has the kids that day.
Suggest a reply-by window: one of you asks by message, the other answers within 3 days. If there’s no answer by then, the one who asked can go ahead.
Keep it to one written channel, so you can both find what was agreed.
Check your parenting plan. If it says nothing, or you can’t agree, a mediator or a family-law professional can help you write it down.

what: That sounds like real burnout, not just a bad week. Thinking about walking away is a sign of how much you’ve been carrying, and it deserves to be taken seriously.
how: Before any big decision, get some real rest if you can. Even a few days off can change how it looks.
Tell your co-founder how tired you are, as a fact, not a verdict: “I’m running on empty, and I need us to change something.”
Look at the load together: one owner and a backup for every recurring job, so it isn’t all on you.
If you’re thinking about leaving, the money, ownership or partnership agreement are a conversation for an accountant or a lawyer.
If the tiredness doesn’t lift, or you feel low most days, talk to your doctor.
script: I’m running on empty, and I’ve even thought about walking away. I don’t want to decide anything this tired. Can we sit down this week and look at who carries what?

cards.name: a family event after a rift
what: A christening, a wedding, a funeral or a holiday can be a way back in, or a hard day. You can go and still keep some things off the table, and you can also say “not yet”.
how: Decide what you’re happy to do (come, stay for the meal) and what you’re not ready to talk about yet.
Say it before the day, kindly and briefly, so nobody is ambushed.
Keep the day about the person it’s for.
Plan an easy way to leave if it gets too much. And if you’re not ready to go, that’s allowed too.

We love that the name matters to you. We’ve chosen a first name from one side and a middle name from the other, so the baby carries both families.

what: Two traditions can mean a full calendar, and some dates move every year. A shared plan for the year helps, so nobody feels their festival came second.
how: Put every festival for the year on one shared calendar, from both traditions, with this year’s dates.
For each one, decide: do we host, visit, or keep it small at home?
Share the work: cooking, presents, travel, cards. Give each job one owner.
Tell both families the plan early, in one go, and keep a few traditions that are just yours.
script: This year we’ll host Eid at ours and go to your parents for Christmas. Next year we’ll swap who travels. Does that feel fair to you?

what: Faith often carries family, memory and meaning, so it makes sense that this feels big. Many interfaith families find a way that honours both, and it usually starts with each of you saying what matters most to you, and why.
how: Each of you names the one or two things that matter most (a ceremony, a holiday, a value, a name) and the things you can be flexible on.
Talk about what you want your child to feel and know, not only which label to choose.
Decide together first, then tell the grandparents as a team: “We’ve decided, and we’d love you to be part of it.”
Make room for both calendars: each tradition’s festivals can be family days, each with its own small traditions.

cards.name: money limits: an agreed limit, or control?
cards.pat: \b(is it|is that|is this|is (he|she|they)( being)?|am i( being)?|are (we|you)|would it be)\b.{0,40}\bcontrolling\b.{0,60}\b(money|buy\w*|bought|spend\w*|purchases?|budget|bank|card|finances?)\b|\b(money|buy\w*|spend\w*|purchases?|budget|finances?)\b.{0,60}\bcontrolling\b|\bcontrolling (about|with|over) (money|spending|finances)\b|\b(check|ask) with me before (he|she|they) (buys?|spends?)\b
what: Agreeing limits on money is normal. Control is something different, and the difference is usually clear once you look at it.
how: Normal: a limit you both agree, that applies to both of you, like “we check with each other before anything over $200.”
Normal: either of you can raise it, change it, or say no, without fear.
Not normal: it’s one-sided (only one of you has to ask), hidden, or punished, with anger, the silent treatment or a card taken away.

Not normal: you have to ask for money you need, explain every receipt, or aren’t allowed to work or see the accounts. If that sounds familiar, the Not safe at home? page lists the signs, and people you can talk to privately.
script: Can we agree one amount where we both check with each other first? Same rule for both of us, and we look at it again in a month.
links: Money together: an agreed limit, or control?
Not safe at home? The signs of control

sides.re: \b(she|he|they|my (fiance|fiancee|partner|wife|husband|girlfriend|boyfriend))\b.{0,40}\b(controlling|approve|approves|check\w*|ask (her|him|them) first|ask permission)\b|\bi (have|need|got) to (ask|explain|justify)\b
what: Feeling watched over every purchase is hard, and it’s worth taking seriously. A limit you both agreed is a normal money plan. Having to get approval for everything, when it only goes one way, is different.
how: Ask yourself the quick check: did we both agree to it? Does it apply to both of us? Can either of us bring it up and change it? Do we both know where the money is?
If the answers are yes, it’s a plan you can tweak together. Suggest one limit for big purchases, and leave the rest alone.
If it’s one-sided, hidden, or you face anger, sulking or a card taken away when you spend, that isn’t a money style. It’s a sign of control.
If you feel afraid to spend, to ask or to say no, the Not safe at home? page lists the signs, and people you can talk to privately.
script: I feel watched when I have to explain small things. Could we agree a limit for big purchases, and leave the rest alone?
links: Not safe at home? The signs

sides.re: \b(is it|would it be|am i( being)?)\b.{0,15}\bcontrolling\b.{0,10}\bif i\b|\bi want to (check|see|look at|go through|approve)\b
what: Fair question, and asking it is a good sign. A check that only goes one way, like you looking at his bank statements every week, leans toward control, even when it comes from worry.
how: Ask what you’re worried about: debt, saving for something, or trust?
Swap the one-way check for something shared: one limit you both agree for big purchases, that applies to both of you.
Or a short money look together once a month, at the same page, with no blame.
If the worry is about trust or hidden debts, say that plainly, as your feeling.
script: I’m not trying to control you. I get anxious about money. Could we agree one limit that applies to both of us, and look at the numbers together once a month?

what: Many couples split shared costs by income instead of half each: each of you pays the same share of what you earn. If he brings home 60% of your joint income, he pays 60% of the rent and shared bills, and you pay 40%.
how: Add up both take-home incomes, and work out each person’s share.
Split rent and shared bills by that share. Keep some personal money each, with no questions asked.
The Lemonade Stand’s Money tab does the sums: add the bills and take-home pay, and tap to split by income.
Look at it again when either income changes.
script: Could we split the rent by income? You’d pay 60% and I’d pay 40%, and we each keep some money that’s just ours.

cards.name: saver and spender: different money styles
cards.pat: \b(i m|im|i am|he|she|he is|she is|theyre|they are|my \w+ is|were|we are|one of us is)( a| the)? (big |natural )?(saver|spender|tightwad|cheapskate)\b|\bsaver\b.{0,30}\bspender\b|\bspender\b.{0,30}\bsaver\b|\b(says|thinks|calls me|told me|tells me) (i m|im|i am) (bad with money|tight|cheap|stingy|irresponsible with money|a spender|too generous)\b|\bbad with money\b|\b(spends?|spending) (too much|so much|all our|all the|way too much)\b|\bmoney styles?\b|\b(different|opposite) (money|spending) (styles?|habits|personalities)\b
what: Money fights are rarely only about money. Savers and spenders usually value different good things: security and freedom, planning and enjoying now. Generosity is a value, not a flaw, and so is caution. The goal is a plan you both chose.
how: Each say what money means to you: safety, freedom, fun, looking after family.
Agree the big numbers together: what you save each month, and a fun amount each of you spends with no questions asked.
Pick a check-first limit that applies to both of you, like any single purchase over $200.
Look at it once a month for 20 minutes, not in the middle of an argument.
If you’re scared of them, not just worried about money, that’s different. The Not safe at home? page can help.
script: I’m a saver; it helps me feel safe. I know you love enjoying life now. Can we agree a fun budget for each of us and a savings amount, and check in monthly?

how: Tell each other the story: what money meant in your family growing up, and one thing you love spending on.
Agree personal money for each of you: a set amount that’s yours, with no questions and no receipts.
One check-in limit that applies to both of you, for big purchases only.
Look at it again every few months, not every time money goes out.
script: Spending on friends and fun is how I enjoy life and show I care. I’d like some money that’s just mine, and I’m happy to agree a limit for big things together.

what: Both things can be true: long hours at work are a real load, and the home still has work that needs doing. The fair way to look at it is the whole load, paid work included, and who has energy for what.
how: Count paid work, travel and home work together for each of you, for one ordinary week.
If the totals are close, the friction is probably about the invisible jobs. If they aren’t, look at what can move, be dropped, or be paid for.
Take one or two home jobs you fully own, start to finish, even with long hours: the weekly shop, Sunday dinner.
Ask what she most needs. Often it’s noticing and planning, not hours.
script: I know I’m working long hours, and I don’t want you carrying home alone. Can we look at both our weeks, work included, and pick two jobs that are fully mine?

what: Showing the whole picture usually works better than arguing about it. When you both look at the same page, it stops being your word against theirs.
how: Write down one ordinary week: paid work, the children, the house, and the thinking jobs, with rough times.
Put it in the Lemonade Stand quick look, so you both see the same picture, as a fact rather than a verdict.
Pick a calm time to look at it together, and ask what her week looks like too.
Start with one ask, not the whole list.

what: Feeling unseen is one of the heaviest parts of this. What goes unnoticed might be the thinking work (remembering, planning), the physical jobs, or your paid work. Often it’s a mix of all three.
how: Write down one week of everything: the jobs, the thinking, and any paid work, with rough times.
Share it as a fact, not a scorecard: “I want us both to see the whole picture.”
Ask for one specific thing: a thank-you, or one job they take over.
The Lemonade Stand shows the split in plain numbers.
script: I don’t need a medal. I’d just like us both to see everything that gets done. Can we look at one week together?

cards.name: twins, toddlers and two tired parents
cards.pat: \b(twins|toddlers|a toddler|our toddler|two under (two|2|three|3)|baby and a toddler|newborn and a toddler|\d ?year ?old twins)\b
what: Toddlers (and two at once even more so) are one of the most tiring stages there is. Both of you being exhausted is normal, not a sign you’re doing it wrong.
how: Protect sleep first: take turns on nights or early mornings, so each of you gets one longer stretch.
Lower the bar on everything else for now: simple meals, less tidying, more help.
Give each daily job one owner (bath time, the nursery bag, the night wake-up), so nobody has to ask.
Ask for specific help: “Could you take them to the park on Saturday morning?”
script: We’re both running on empty. Can we take turns on the early mornings, so each of us gets one lie-in this weekend?
