cards.name: feeling like a burden when you’re ill
cards.pat: \bburden\b.{0,40}\b(my )?(husband|wife|partner|boyfriend|girlfriend|carer|caregiver|spouse)\b|\b(husband|wife|partner|boyfriend|girlfriend|carer|caregiver|spouse)\b.{0,40}\bburden\b|\b(ill|illness|sick|disabled|disability|chronic\w*|chronically ill|pain|me cfs|mecfs|cfs|long covid|fibromyalgia|fibro|lupus|ms|crohns?|endometriosis|arthritis)\b.{0,60}\bburden\b|\bburden\b.{0,60}\b(ill|illness|sick|disabled|disability|chronic\w*|chronically ill|pain|me cfs|mecfs|cfs|long covid|fibromyalgia|fibro|lupus|ms|crohns?|endometriosis|arthritis)\b
what: Being ill isn’t being a burden. You’re a partner who is ill, and what you bring to the relationship isn’t measured in chores. Feeling this way is very common, and it’s worth saying out loud to them.
how: Tell them the feeling, not only the guilt: “I feel like a burden, and I hate it.” Most partners want to hear that.
Share by energy, not hours: each of you does what you can on the energy you have that day.
Keep a list of things you can own from bed or the sofa: planning meals, online orders, birthdays, calls.
Make sure the carer side has support too, so neither of you runs on empty.
If the feeling turns into thoughts that they’d be better off without you, tell your doctor or someone you trust today.
script: I feel like a burden, and I hate it. Can we talk about what I can still own, so it feels more like a team?
links: When one of you is ill or disabled
Caring for someone you love (their side)

cards.name: sharing the load when one of you is ill
cards.pat: \b(ill|illness|sick|disabled|disability|chronic\w*|chronically ill|pain|me cfs|mecfs|cfs|long covid|fibromyalgia|fibro|lupus|ms|crohns?|endometriosis|arthritis)\b.{0,60}\b(chores|split|share|fair\w*|housework|bed|energy|bad days?|do my part|help)\b|\bsome days i (cant|can t) get out of bed\b|\b(from|in) bed on (bad|my bad|low) days\b|\bfrom bed\b.{0,30}\b(bad days?|help|do)\b|\bbad days?\b.{0,30}\b(from bed|in bed|energy)\b|\bspoons?\b.{0,20}\b(theory|left|energy)\b
what: When one of you is ill or disabled, a fair split is about energy, not hours. You still count, and there’s more you can own than you might think.
how: Rate your energy each morning (good, low, bed day) and share it, so plans fit the day.
Own jobs you can do from bed or a chair on bad days: meal planning and online shopping, bills, booking appointments, birthdays and cards, calls and admin.
On good days, resist doing everything. Pacing protects tomorrow.
Agree what gets dropped or simplified on bad days, so it isn’t a fresh decision each time.
Count the carer’s load too, and find them some support.
script: Today’s a bed day for me. I can do the online shop and the calls from here. Could you do the cooking tonight?

cards.name: whether you have to forgive
cards.pat: \b(is it|its|it is|is it ever) (ok|okay|alright|fine|wrong|bad) (to |if i )?(not|dont|don t|never) (to )?forgive\w*\b|\bnot (ready|able|willing) to forgive\b|\b(cant|can t|dont want to|do not want to) forgive\b
what: Yes. Forgiving is yours to give or not, and it can’t be rushed. Reconciling is a separate choice. You can let go of anger without letting someone back in, and you can be in touch without saying what happened was okay.
how: Notice what you actually want: peace for yourself, a relationship again, an apology, or distance.
You can say “I’m not ready” and leave the door where it is, open or closed.
If anger is eating at you, talking it through with a counsellor or someone you trust helps, for you, not for them.
script: I’m not ready to talk about it yet. I’ll let you know if that changes.
links: “I’m not ready”, and “I don’t have to”

cards.name: whether you have to reconcile
cards.pat: \b(do|must|should) i (have to |really have to |need to )?(reconcile|make up|forgive|make peace)\b.{0,30}\b(with )?(my )?(brother|sister|sibling\w*|family|dad|father|mum|mom|mother|parents?|him|her|them)?\b|\bhave i got to (reconcile|forgive)\b
what: No, you don’t have to. Forgiving is yours to give or not, and reconciling is a separate choice. Some people reconnect, some keep a polite distance, and some stay apart. Each can be the right answer.
how: Notice what you actually want: peace for yourself, a relationship again, an apology, or distance.
If you want to try, start small, with no demand attached: a card, a short message.
If you don’t, you can still let go of some of the anger, for your own sake.
script: I’m not ready to talk about it yet. I’ll let you know if that changes.

cards.name: the favourite child
cards.pat: \b(was|is|were|always been) (always )?(the |mum |mom |dad |their |her |his )?(favou?rite|golden child|favou?red one|favou?red)\b|\bfavou?ritism\b|\bgolden child\b|\b(dad|mum|mom|father|mother|parents?)\b.{0,25}\b(always )?(loved|liked|preferred|favou?red|spoiled|spoilt) (him|her|them|my (brother|sister)) (more|best|better)\b|\b(loved|liked|preferred) (him|her|my (brother|sister)) (more|best)\b
what: Growing up as the less-favoured child leaves a real mark, and it can come back hard as adults, especially around a parent getting older, a will, or a loss. Your feelings about it make sense.
how: It can help to keep two hurts apart: what your parent did, and how things are with your sibling now.
Say what you needed, at least to yourself: “I needed to feel I mattered as much.”
If you talk to your parent or sibling, describe your experience, not their motives: “I often felt second.”
Old family roles return fast at family events. It’s okay to respond as the adult you are now, and it’s okay to want contact, or not yet.
script: I often felt second growing up. I’m not blaming you. I’d like us to talk about it one day.
I’m not ready to talk about it yet. I’ll let you know when I am.

cards.name: when a sibling doesn’t reply
what: Silence after a long gap often means “I don’t know what to say yet”, not “no”. Give it time: weeks, not days.
how: One gentle follow-up, at most: “No need to reply. I just wanted you to know the door is open.” Then stop.
Don’t send a flood. Many messages can feel like pressure, even when they come from love.
If there’s a family event coming, like a christening, you can still invite them once, with no pressure, and let the day be about the child.
You can do your part well and still not get the answer you hoped for. That isn’t a failure. The rest is their choice.
script: I know it’s been a long time, and I’m sorry for my part in it. The christening is on the 14th. No pressure to reply, but I’d really like you there.
No need to reply. I just wanted you to know the door is open.

what: Years of silence can feel impossible to cross, and it’s rarely one person’s fault. Reaching out usually works best small, warm, and with no demand attached.
how: Start with a short message that asks for nothing: “I’ve been thinking about you. I’d like to be in touch, if you would. No pressure.”
Don’t open with the old argument. If you want to talk about it, ask later: “Would you be willing to talk about what happened, one day?”
Expect a slow reply, or none. That’s their choice, and it isn’t the end of the story.
Decide in advance what you’d be happy with: cards at birthdays, a coffee, or more.
script: I’ve been thinking about you, and I miss having you in my life. I’d like to be in touch, if you would. No pressure to reply.

cards.name: care you show by doing
cards.pat: \b(dont|do not|never|rarely|didnt|did not) (say|says|said) (i love you|love you|love)\b|\b(dont|do not|never|rarely) (say|says|said|tell|show) (it|love|feelings|our feelings) (out loud|aloud|in words)\b|\b(we|they|my family|our family|my parents|my (dad|mum|mom|husband|wife))\b.{0,30}\b(dont|do not|never|rarely) (tell each other|tell me|tell us) (i love you|love you|that they love)\b|\b(show|shows|showing|showed) (love|care|affection) (by|through|with) (doing|food|cooking|acts|actions|deeds|fixing)\b|\bnot (very )?(expressive|affectionate|touchy feely) (family|culture|people)\b|\bnot good with words\b|\bbad with words\b|\bnot a words person\b
what: Care you show by doing counts. Many families and cultures show love with food, practical help, time or small gifts more than with words. Cooking a meal, fixing the car or driving someone somewhere can say “I love you” as clearly as words.
how: Notice the care that’s shown by doing, and thank it in words: “I noticed you cleaned the kitchen. Thank you. I see it.”
Tell the other person, once, what your actions mean: “When I cook your favourite food, it means I care about you.”
Ask what makes them feel cared for, then do one of those things this week.
Problems start only when one person waits for words and the other gives actions. Neither is wrong.
script: I don’t always say it, but when I fix things in the house, I am doing it for you.

what: Sunday evenings are hard for many parents and kids. The first hour in a quiet home is often the hardest, and it usually eases as you build a routine around it.
how: Keep the last hour calm and simple: a meal, a show, packing the bag together.
Say when you’ll next see them, and when you’ll talk before then.
Plan something for yourself afterwards, like a call with a friend or a walk.
Stay close between visits: a short call at the same time each week, a photo, a question about the thing they care about.

what: When the children leave, the house can go quiet in a way that’s surprisingly hard, and many couples find they’ve been talking mostly about the kids for years. It’s a normal stage, and a chance to rebuild what’s just yours.
how: Name it together: “It’s so quiet. I miss them, and I don’t quite know what we do now.”
Start one small ritual for the two of you: a weekly walk, a new place to eat, cooking something new.
Ask each other a real question that isn’t about the kids: “What do you want the next ten years to look like?”
Stay close to the kids in a way that doesn’t lean on them: a weekly call, a visit each term.
script: It’s so quiet without them. I miss them. Shall we try something new together this weekend, just us?

cards.pat: \bi (dont|don t|do not|really dont|never|hate to|hate) (really )?(like|enjoy|want to|feel comfortable|talking|talk)\b.{0,15}\b(talking|to talk|speaking|sharing|opening up|talk)? ?about (my |our )?(feelings|emotions)\b|\b(im|i m|i am) not (a|much of a) (talker|feelings person|feelings kind of person)\b|\btalking about (feelings|emotions) (is not|isnt|is not really) (for me|my thing)\b
what: That’s okay. Many people show care by doing rather than talking: fixing things, cooking, turning up. That counts, and you don’t have to become someone else.
how: Care you show by doing counts. Now and then, name it: “I fixed the shelf because I wanted you to have one less thing.”
You don’t need a big talk. Side by side works better: a walk, a drive, cooking together.
If your partner wants more words, try one small line a day: one fact and one feeling.
Many people were never taught to talk about feelings. That isn’t a problem with you.

cards.name: talking about feelings

what: Many people were never taught to talk about feelings. That isn’t a problem with you, and you can build the words slowly, without a big talk.
how: Start tiny: one fact and one feeling a day. “Work was long. I’m tired, and glad to be home.”
Use simple feeling words: glad, tired, worried, proud, sad, cross. One is enough.
Talk side by side, not face to face: on a walk, in the car, while cooking.
If you show care by doing, say it once in words too: “I fixed the shelf because I want you to have one less thing.”

how: Start with one sentence about one feeling, to one person you trust.
If words won’t come, name it in the body first: “There’s a knot in my stomach about this.”
Write it down before you say it. That counts.

cards.name: small talk at work
cards.pat: \b(hate|dread|bad at|struggle with|cant do|can t do|don t get|dont get|awful at|hard)\b.{0,15}\bsmall talk\b.{0,40}\b(work|office|colleagues?|coworkers?|say|break room|kitchen)\b|\bsmall talk\b.{0,30}\b(at work|in the office|with (colleagues|coworkers))\b|\bwhat (do|should) i say\b.{0,30}\bsmall talk\b
what: Small talk is hard for lots of people. It helps to have three stock lines ready, and it’s fine to keep it to one exchange.
how: Three lines that work almost anywhere: “How was your weekend?”, “Busy day?”, “Anything good planned?”
Answer with one fact and one question back: “Quiet, thanks. Did you get away?”
It’s fine to keep it to one exchange, then close kindly: “Right, back to it. Good to see you.”
Nobody is grading it. The point is a friendly signal, not a real conversation.
script: Good, thanks. Busy day for you?
Right, I’d better get back to it. Good to catch you.

cards.name: why small talk is hard
cards.pat: \bwhy (is|do|does|are)\b.{0,40}\bsmall talk\b|\bsmall talk\b.{0,30}\b(so hard|hard|exhausting|difficult|draining|pointless|tiring)\b|\b(chatting|chat|talking) about the weather\b.{0,30}\b(hard|exhausting|difficult|pointless)\b|\bwhy (do|does) (some )?people (find|hate)\b.{0,30}\b(weather|small talk|chit ?chat)\b
what: Small talk is hard for lots of people, and for many autistic people especially, because its rules are unwritten: the words matter less than the signal underneath (“I’m friendly, we’re fine”). If you take words literally, or find guessing tiring, it can feel pointless and draining. That’s a difference in wiring, not a failing.
how: It works more like a ritual than a conversation: a short, friendly signal both people recognise.
Having three stock lines ready takes most of the guessing out.
It’s fine to keep it to one exchange, then close kindly.
The double empathy idea explains why it’s hard both ways: people wired differently misread each other, not just one side.
links: Wired differently: the double empathy problem

cards.name: “when you get a chance”
cards.pat: \bwhen you (get|have) a (chance|minute|moment|sec|second)\b|\b(asap|when you can|at some point|no rush|whenever you can)\b.{0,40}\b(deadline|mean|by when|how long)\b|\bwhat deadline (does|is)\b
what: “When you get a chance” has no deadline, so it’s fair to ask for one. Most people mean “soon, but not urgent”, often within a few days.
how: Ask straight away, in one line: “Is end of day Friday okay?”
If they say “whenever”, pick a time and say it: “I’ll have it to you by Thursday.”
Reply in writing, so you both have the date.
script: Happy to. Is end of day Friday okay?

cards.name: why people don’t say what they mean
cards.pat: \bwhy (do|dont|don t|cant|can t|wont|won t) (people|they|some people|others|he|she|everyone)\b.{0,15}\b(say what (they|he|she) (mean|want)|just say (it|what they mean)|say (it|things) (straight|directly|plainly)|be (direct|clear))\b|\b(hints?|hinting)\b.{0,20}\b(instead of|rather than)\b.{0,20}\b(saying|asking)\b
what: Often because saying it straight feels risky. People soften what they mean to be polite, to protect the relationship, or because their family or culture taught them to hint. The meaning moves into tone and context, which is easy to miss, especially between people who are wired differently.
how: If you’re not sure what someone meant, ask kindly: “Do you mean you’d like me to do it today?”
Say your own asks plainly, with a warm tone: “Could you do the dishes tonight?”
A hint isn’t a lie; it’s a different code. The Carrier Wave Decoder helps you read the message under the words.
The double empathy idea explains why both sides misread each other, not just one.
links: Rewind the talk (the Carrier Wave Decoder)
Wired differently: the double empathy problem

cards.name: is autism a disorder
cards.pat: \bis (autism|being autistic|adhd) (a |an )?(disorder|disease|illness|mental illness|disability|condition|defect)\b|\b(autism|adhd) (a |an )?(disorder|disease|illness) or (a )?(difference|different)\b
what: It depends who you ask, and both answers point at something real. Medical manuals list autism as a developmental condition (the diagnosis is called autism spectrum disorder), and that diagnosis is what opens the door to support. Many autistic people and researchers describe it instead as a difference in how the brain works: a disability in a world built for other wiring, not something broken. This site takes the second view: different wiring, not a fault.
how: Autistic people vary as much as anyone: strengths, struggles and support needs differ a lot.
What helps most is usually the setup: clear asks, less sensory overload, and fewer unwritten rules.

cards.name: asking for what helps at work
cards.pat: \b(noise|noisy|loud|too loud|sound)\b.{0,30}\b(at work|office|workplace|open plan|my desk)\b|\b(office|workplace|open plan|work)\b.{0,20}\b(is |s |gets )?(too |so |really )?(loud|noisy)\b|\bquiet (break|space|room|corner)\b.{0,20}\b(at work|work|office)\b|\b(need|want|take) a quiet break\b|\b(manager|boss|supervisor|team lead|line manager)\b.{0,40}\b(vague|unclear|write (it |things |them )?down|written|in writing|instructions)\b|\b(written|clear|clearer) instructions\b|\b(tell|telling|disclose|disclosing|say)\b.{0,20}\b(my )?(manager|boss|work|employer|hr|colleagues|team)\b.{0,20}\b(i m|im|i am|that i m|that im|that i am|about my|about being|im an?) (autistic|autism|adhd|neurodivergent|dyslexic|on the spectrum)\b|\bstep away when it (gets )?(loud|noisy|too much)\b|\b(reasonable )?adjustments\b.{0,20}\b(work|autism|autistic|adhd)\b|\baccommodations?\b.{0,20}\b(work|autism|autistic|adhd)\b
what: Asking for what helps you work well is reasonable, and clear, specific asks usually land best. You don’t have to name a diagnosis to ask. In many places the law asks employers to consider reasonable adjustments for disabled staff, and autism can count.
how: Noise: ask for a quieter spot, noise-cancelling headphones, or short quiet breaks: “When it gets loud I need ten minutes somewhere quiet, then I’m back and focused.”
Instructions: ask for tasks in writing, with what “done” looks like and the deadline.
Telling your manager you’re autistic is your choice. If you do, keep it practical: what it means for you at work, and two or three things that help.
Afterwards, put what you agreed in a short email, so it’s remembered.
script: I work best with written instructions. Could you send tasks by email, with what done looks like and the deadline?
I’m autistic. For me that means noise drains me fast, and clear written steps help me do my best work. Could we try a quiet break and written tasks?
scriptLabels: If you choose to tell your manager

cards.name: being told you’re rude when you’re direct
cards.pat: \b(they|people|everyone|my (boss|manager|team|coworkers?|colleagues?))\b.{0,15}\b(say|says|said|think|thinks|tell me|told me|complain)\b.{0,10}\b(that )?(i m|im|i am|i was|i come across( as)?|i sound)\b.{0,10}\b(rude|blunt|too direct|harsh|cold|abrupt|unfriendly)\b
what: Being direct isn’t the same as being rude, and you don’t have to change your whole style. A short line that explains your style often clears it up.
how: Say it once, plainly: you’re direct because you want to be clear.
Ask for specifics: which message, which words? Then you can decide what, if anything, to change.
If you like, add one line of thanks or a reason to a short message. That’s optional, not a fix for you.
If you’re autistic, you can ask for adjustments, like instructions in writing. The law in many places asks employers to consider reasonable adjustments.
script: Thanks for telling me. I’m direct because I want to be clear, not unkind. If something lands badly, tell me and I’ll rephrase it.

what: With three of you, a calm message works best when it’s about the house, not one person, and asks for a fix and a time, not a verdict.
how: Keep the message short and about the job, not about who forgot.
Suggest a fix, not a complaint: a rota, or one owner each week.
Ask for ten minutes in person. Tense things go better face to face than in the group chat.
If one person is the issue, talk to them on their own, kindly, first.

cards.name: when one housemate has much longer hours
what: It can, yes. Fair doesn’t have to mean equal: some houses split jobs by the time each person has, and some keep it equal and swap in heavy weeks. What matters is that all of you agree the rule.
how: Say the hours out loud: lab, work, travel. It’s easier to agree a rule when everyone sees the same week.
Pick a rule together: equal jobs, jobs by time available, or a swap during deadline weeks.
The busy person can own jobs that fit their week, like the weekend clean or the online shop.
Look at it again in a month.
script: I’ve got a heavy month at the lab. Could I take the jobs I can do at weekends, and do more again after the deadline?

what: Yes, a rota is fine, and lots of shared houses use one. The key is that each job still has one clear owner each week, so nothing falls between people.
how: Give each job one owner for a set stretch, then rotate: weekly or monthly, whatever suits the house.
Write the rota where everyone sees it: the fridge, or pinned in the group chat.
Agree a clear handover when it rotates: who’s on bins from Monday.
Look at it in the weekly house meeting. If someone keeps missing a turn, talk about the job, not the person.
script: Can we do a rota where each of us owns a few jobs for a month, then we swap? I’ll put it on the fridge.

what: Bins are the classic shared-home job: everyone assumes someone else will do it, so it lands on whoever minds first. It’s usually not laziness, just a job with no owner.
how: Make a quick list of the shared jobs, bins included, and give each one an owner or a weekly rota.
Put it where all of you can see it: the fridge, or a pinned message in the group chat.
A ten-minute house meeting once a week: start with the list, not with who forgot.
Raise it as a house thing, for any of you, not a complaint about one person.

cards.name: bringing it up when you hate confrontation
what: Lots of people would rather put up with something for months than have one awkward talk. A small, calm talk early is kinder, to both of you, than a big one later.
how: Pick a calm time: not when they walk in with their guest, and not late at night.
A text is fine to start: “Can we talk about something small tonight?”
One topic, and one clear ask. Say what you need and ask what works for them.
Talk about the room, not the person: “The room is getting crowded” lands better than “You’re so inconsiderate.”
script: Hey, can we find ten minutes this week to agree a few room things, like guests staying over? Nothing’s wrong, I’d just rather we sort it early than let it get awkward.
This is a bit awkward, but I’d rather say it now than let it build up. Can we agree on a few room rules?

cards.name: if your roommate reacts badly
what: If she gets annoyed when you bring it up, that doesn’t mean you were wrong to ask. A bit of defensiveness at first is common, and it often settles after a day.
how: Stay calm and repeat your one ask. You don’t have to argue every point.
Say you’re not attacking her: it’s about the room, not about her as a person.
If it gets heated, pause and pick it up tomorrow: “Let’s leave it for tonight and talk tomorrow.”
If nothing changes, your RA or housing office can help you both write a room agreement.
script: I’m not saying you’re a bad roommate. I just need the room to myself some nights. Can we find something that works for both of us?

what: With a baby, the nights are a real job. Many couples split the night into blocks, so each of you gets one long stretch of sleep, rather than both waking for every feed.
how: Split the night in two blocks, for example 9 pm to 2 am and 2 am to 7 am, and swap now and then. Count night feeds inside the on-call block, not on top of a full day.
Ask for one thing, clearly: “Can you take the 5 a.m. feed?” works better than “I never get any sleep.”
No big talks in the night. If one starts at 3 a.m., park it and say when you’ll come back to it, like nap time tomorrow.
Put the night blocks on your list of jobs, each with an owner. The Who does what? quick look has new-baby jobs, and you can add your own.

cards.pat: \bget (him|her|them|my \w+) to (stay|finish|keep talking|come back)\b|\bfinish the (conversation|argument|talk)\b|\b(make|keep) (him|her|them) (stay|talk)\b
what: You can’t make someone stay in a talk when they’re flooded, but you can make coming back easy and certain. Asking “when will we come back to it?” instead of “stay and finish” is usually what gets the talk back.
how: Ask for a time, not an answer: “Okay. When shall we pick this up?” A named time is your guarantee it isn’t being dropped.
Let them go, and don’t follow; following tells their body the danger isn’t over.
Use the wait for yourself: write down the one thing you most want them to understand.
Come back to one topic only, and let them speak first.
script: Okay, take your break. When shall we pick this up? I want to hear you, and I want us to finish it.
plain: You can’t make them stay.
Ask: “When can we talk again?”
Let them go. Don’t follow.
Talk again at that time.

cards.name: my partner doesn't back me up
cards.pat: \b(doesn t|doesnt|won t|wont|never|didn t|didnt) (back|backs) me up\b|\b(undermine\w*|takes? (their|the kids|her|his) side)\b.{0,40}\b(kids?|son|daughter|step\w*|in front of)\b|\bnot on the same page\b.{0,30}\b(kids|rules|discipline|parenting)\b
what: Feeling unbacked in front of the kids is lonely, and it’s one of the most common snags in stepfamilies and in any family with two parents. It usually means the rules weren’t agreed in private first, not that your partner is against you.
how: Agree the few rules that matter most in private, at a calm time, before they come up with the kids.
Agree a sign or a line for “let’s talk about this later”, so neither of you argues it out in front of them.
In a stepfamily, the parent usually leads on discipline at first while the stepparent builds the relationship; backing up means supporting that, not enforcing alone.
Afterwards, talk about it as a gap in the plan, not as betrayal.
script: I felt on my own in front of the kids earlier. Can we agree the few rules that matter to us both, so we back each other up next time?
plain: Agree the rules together in private.
Then support each other in front of the kids.
Talk later, not in front of them.

cards.name: how much family support is reasonable
cards.pat: \bhow much (is (it )?(reasonable|normal|fair|ok|okay)|should (i|we|she|he)) (to )?(send|give)\b|\bwhat (percent\w*|percentage|share|amount)\b.{0,40}\b(send|give|income)\b.{0,40}\b(family|parents|mum|mom|mother|home)\b|\b(percent\w*|percentage) of (our|my|his|her) income\b
what: There’s no right number for everyone; it depends on your income, your family’s needs and what you both feel secure with. What helps most is choosing the number together, with a simple method, instead of arguing month by month.
how: Add up what goes now, and fix the basics first: rent, food, bills and an amount of savings you both want.
From what’s left, agree a monthly family-support line, and write it down.

For example: if you take home £3,000 a month and rent, food, bills and the savings you want come to £2,500, a family line of up to about £300 still leaves a cushion for surprises. The right number is the one you can both keep up without dread.
Agree an emergency rule (for example: a phone call before any extra amount above a set figure).
Look at it again twice a year, or when income or family needs change.
Put it in the Lemonade Stand’s Money tab as an agreed amount, so it is never a debt between you.
script: Could we sit down with the numbers on Sunday, put the basics and our savings first, and then agree the family amount together?
plain: There is no one right number.
First pay rent, food, bills and savings.
Then agree a family amount together.
Look at it again twice a year.

what: Missing work is common and real: work gave structure, people and a sense of being useful. Most people need to rebuild those on purpose after retiring, and it takes a few months.
how: Pick one thing with a regular time and other people: a class, a club, volunteering, a part-time role. Good places to ask: your library, a place of worship, the local council or community centre, a men’s shed or walking group, or a volunteering website for your area.
Use something you’re good at: fixing, teaching, organizing, cooking for others.
Keep a lunch or call going with a few old colleagues.
Move most days, outside if you can.
At home, take one whole job that’s completely yours.
If you feel low most days for more than a couple of weeks, talk to your doctor.

Find one regular thing with other people.
Use a skill you have.
Take one job at home that is yours.

cards.name: being autistic is not something wrong with you
cards.pat: \b(i m|im|i am|ive been diagnosed|i ve been diagnosed|i was diagnosed|just diagnosed|found out i m|found out im)\b.{0,20}\b(autistic|autism|on the spectrum|asd|adhd|audhd)\b.{0,60}\b(wrong with me|broken|normal|faulty|a problem|bad person|defective)\b|\b(wrong with me|am i broken)\b.{0,30}\b(autis\w*|on the spectrum|adhd)\b
what: No. Autism is a different way of being wired, not a fault. Many autistic people find the hard part is a world built for other wiring, not anything wrong in them.
how: Wired Differently explains autism, ADHD and other wiring in plain words, as differences, not flaws.
If work is where it’s hardest, “If you’re autistic at work” has plain sentences for written asks, quiet breaks and being read as rude.
A Wiring Card can sum up how you work best, to share if and when you choose.
If you feel low most days, talk to your doctor too. That’s about how you’re feeling, not about being autistic.

cards.name: wondering if something is wrong with you
cards.pat: \b(is (there )?)?something wrong with me\b|\bwhat'?s wrong with me\b|\bwhat is wrong with me\b|\bam i (broken|the problem|normal|crazy|a bad (person|partner|husband|wife))\b|\bi feel (so )?(low|down|useless|empty|flat|worthless)\b
what: Asking that usually means you’re going through a hard patch, not that you’re broken. Big changes like retiring, a new baby, a move or a loss knock most people off balance for a while, and feeling low, flat or in the way is a common part of that.
how: Be as kind to yourself as you would be to a friend saying the same thing.
Say it out loud to one person you trust: “I’ve been feeling low lately.”
Give each day a small shape: one thing with other people, one thing you’re good at, some time outside.
Notice what helps even a little, and do more of that.
If you feel low most days for more than a couple of weeks, or it’s hard to get through the day, talk to your doctor. That’s a normal, sensible step.
script: I’ve been feeling a bit lost lately. I don’t need you to fix it, I just wanted you to know.
plain: Nothing is wrong with you for feeling this way.
Big changes make most people feel low for a while.
Tell one person you trust.
If it lasts more than two weeks, see your doctor.

cards.name: stopping losing your temper
cards.pat: \bhow (do|can|could) i (stop|quit) (losing|lose) (my temper|it|my cool|my rag)\b|\bi (keep|always|still) (losing|lose|lost) (it|my temper|my cool|my rag)\b|^(i (keep )?(losing|lose|lost) (it|my temper))$|^my temper$|\b(i have|i ve got|ive got|got) (a |an )?(bad |terrible |short |quick )?(temper|anger (problem|issue|issues)|anger management (problem|issue))\b|^(an )?anger (problem|issue|issues)$|\bmy anger (problem|issue|issues|is out of control|scares me)\b|\b(control|manage) my (temper|anger)\b|\bshort fuse\b|\bi (keep|always|ve been|have been|m always|am always|still|constantly) (snapping|snap|shouting|yelling|being short|getting short|blowing up) (at|with) (my )?(wife|husband|partner|kids|children|family|son|daughter|everyone|them|the kids)\b
what: Wanting to change it is the biggest step, and it can change.
how: Stop and step back as soon as you notice your voice going up.
Say what’s happening: “I’m getting too loud. I’m going to take a breath.”
Breathe for one minute, in for 4 and out for 6, and don’t go back until your body has slowed down.
Make it right: “I’m sorry I yelled. That wasn’t fair to you.” Then say what you’ll do differently.
Get support for yourself too: your doctor, an Employee Assistance Program, or an anger-management group or counsellor.
script: I’m sorry I lost my temper. That wasn’t fair to you, and it wasn’t your fault. I’m working on stepping away before I get loud.

cards.name: yelling at your partner
cards.pat: \bi (yell|yelled|shout|shouted|scream|screamed|lost my temper|lose my temper|swore) (at|with) (my )?(wife|husband|partner|girlfriend|boyfriend|spouse|fiance|fiancee)\b|\bi (keep |always )?(lose|losing) my temper with (my )?(wife|husband|partner|girlfriend|boyfriend)\b
what: Noticing it is the first step, and wanting to change matters. Yelling usually comes when stress is already high and there’s no pause plan, but it still hurts the person on the other end, so it’s worth working on.
how: Agree a pause word together on a calm day: either of you can say it, and you step away for twenty minutes, then come back at a time you name.
When you feel it rising, say “I’m getting too loud, I’m going to take a breath,” and step away before the words come out.
Afterwards, apologise for the specific thing, without a “but”, and say what you’ll do differently.
If it happens most days, or anyone at home is afraid of you, get support for yourself: your doctor or a counsellor who does anger management.
script: I yelled at you. That wasn’t fair, and it wasn’t about you. Next time I’ll step away when I feel it rising, and come back in twenty minutes.
plain: Agree a pause word.
Step away before you shout.
Say sorry for the specific thing.
Get help if it happens a lot.

cards.name: coming out when family may react badly
what: That fear makes sense, and it’s worth planning around. Many families come round in time, even when the first reaction is hard. But if you rely on your family for a home, money or a visa, or you think they might cut you off or hurt you, plan first.
how: Your own money: a bank account and a phone in your own name, and some savings if you can.
Somewhere to go if a talk goes badly: a friend’s sofa, a way home.
You can wait. There’s no deadline, and telling a sibling or a friend first is a real step.
Support: in the US, the LGBT National Help Center on 1-888-843-4564; in the UK, Switchboard on 0800 0119 100. If you’re afraid of violence, or of being forced into anything, see Not safe at home?

what: Feeling like a told-off kid is a horrible feeling, and it makes sense if criticism hits you hard. Often the other person was worried about the thing (like a safety risk), and the words came out sharper than they meant.
how: Take a breath before you answer. Ten minutes is fine.
Read the message for the worry underneath: “Someone sent me this” in the message checker shows what they may have meant, and gives you a calm reply.
Say how it landed, without arguing about the fact: “You’re right that it matters. The way it was said made me feel like a kid.”
Agree a system for the thing itself (a stove check by the door, a reminder), so it doesn’t keep coming back as criticism.
If your wiring is different (ADHD, autistic or otherwise), swapping Wiring Cards shows how each of you takes in words.

how: Bring it up privately first, calmly, and soon: “Hey, rent was due on the 1st and I haven’t seen your share yet. Is everything okay?”
Assume there may be a reason, and ask for a date: “When do you think you can send it?”
Agree a simple house rule for everyone: rent and bills go in by a set day, into one place, and anyone who’s going to be late says so before the day.
Write the shared bills down so everyone sees the same numbers: the Lemonade Stand’s Money tab works for three or more people.

how: Pick one of these and agree it together: a small kitty everyone tops up monthly, a rota for who buys this month, or one owner who buys and everyone pays back by a set day.
Keep a shared list (a note in the group chat) so whoever is at the shop can see what’s low.
Add the supplies to the Lemonade Stand’s Money tab, so the spend is visible and split fairly.

cards.name: making friends as an autistic adult
cards.pat: \b(make|making|find|finding|keep|keeping) (new )?friends\b.{0,40}\b(autis\w*|aspergers?|asd|neurodivergent|adhd|audhd)\b|\b(autis\w*|aspergers?|neurodivergent|audhd)\b.{0,40}\b(make|making|find|finding|keep|keeping) (new )?friends\b
what: Lots of autistic adults find friendship easier around a shared interest than through small talk. Regular beats big: the same faces, in the same place, again and again.
how: Start from an interest: a club, a class, a game night, an online group or a volunteering shift. The activity does the talking.
Go regularly. A weekly thing with the same people builds friendships faster than one big night out.
Choose what suits you: one-to-one or small groups, quieter places, plans made ahead.
Say what works for you: “I’m better at texting than calls.” The right friends will be glad to know.
Look for other autistic or neurodivergent people too. Many find it a relief to be understood without translating.
script: I really enjoyed that. Would you like to come again next week? I like making plans ahead.

cards.name: ADHD with friends, and remembering what people tell you
cards.pat: \badhd\b.{0,40}\b(friend|friends|friendships?|social)\b|\bhow (do|can) i remember (what|things) (my )?(friends|people|they|others) (tell|told|say|said)\b|\bremember (my )?(friends|people).{0,20}\b(birthdays|news|names)\b|\bforget (my )?(friends|people).{0,20}\b(birthdays|news|names)\b
what: With ADHD, forgetting what friends told you is usually about working memory, not about caring less. Friends feel it as “you weren’t listening”, so a small system goes a long way.
how: Write it down straight away: a note on that friend’s contact (“new job at the bakery, starts Monday”).
Put birthdays and big dates in your calendar with a reminder two days before.
Repeat the key bit back while they’re talking (“So the interview is Thursday?”). It helps it stick and shows you’re listening.
When you do forget, own it plainly: “Sorry I forgot your interview. That’s on me. How did it go?” Skip “you know how I am”.
Tell close friends how you work, once: “If I don’t ask about something, it’s memory, not that I don’t care. Remind me any time.”
script: Sorry I forgot to ask about your interview. That’s on me. How did it go?
plain: Write it down right away.
Put birthdays in your calendar.
Repeat the main thing back.
If you forget, say sorry plainly.

cards.name: ADHD at work
cards.pat: \badhd\b.{0,40}\b(at work|work|job|office|developer|engineer|manager|boss|meetings?|deadlines?)\b|\b(at work|my job)\b.{0,40}\badhd\b
what: Plenty of people with ADHD do very well at work with a few supports that match how their attention works. It’s about the setup, not effort.
how: Make the invisible visible: one task list you trust, deadlines in your calendar, and reminders for handovers.
Protect focus time: block it out, mute notifications, and batch messages.
Ask for asks in writing after meetings (“Could you drop the actions in the chat?”).
Share a short Wiring Card with your team or manager if you’re comfortable: how you work best, and what helps.
Disclosure is your choice. Where it applies, workplace adjustments are available; a doctor or HR can explain options.
script: I work best with the ask in writing. Could you drop the actions in the chat after the meeting?
plain: Keep one task list.
Block focus time.
Ask for actions in writing.

cards.name: stuck in the middle of your parents
cards.pat: \bstuck (in the middle|between) (of )?(my )?(mum|mom|dad|parents|stepdad|stepmom|stepfather|stepmother)\b|\b(mum|mom|dad|parents?|stepdad|stepmom) (makes?|made|making|wants?|tries to make) me (pick|choose|take) (a )?sides?\b|\b(make|makes|made) me (pick|choose|take) (a )?side between\b|\bin the middle of (my )?(mum|mom|dad|parents)( and (my )?(stepdad|stepmom|dad|mum|mom))?\b
what: Being stuck in the middle of the adults you love is really hard, and it’s not your job to fix their relationship. You’re allowed to love both of them, and you don’t have to pick a side.
how: When one of them complains about the other to you, you can say a short line and change the subject.
If they ask you to pass on messages, it’s okay to say no: “Can you tell them yourself?”
Give yourself space when it’s loud: headphones, your room, a walk, a friend’s house.
Tell one adult you trust how it feels: a relative, a teacher or a school counselor.
If the fighting ever scares you, or anyone gets hurt, that’s more than arguing. You can ask for help even if nobody is hurting you directly.
script: I love you both and I’m not picking a side. Please don’t ask me to.
Can you tell them yourself? I don’t want to be the messenger.
plain: It is not your job to fix it.
You can love both of them.
You do not have to pick a side.

what: Fighting with a brother or sister is really common, especially when you share space and get compared. It doesn’t mean you don’t care about each other.
how: Agree a few simple rules for shared stuff and your own space (knock first, ask before borrowing).
When it heats up, walk away for ten minutes instead of having the last word.
If you keep getting blamed, tell a parent calmly, at a calm time: “Can we work out a fair rule for this?”
Find one thing you both like (a game, a show) and do it together sometimes.

Can we agree a rule for my stuff? Ask me first, and I’ll ask you first too.

cards.name: a young person looking for someone to talk to

what: It’s good that you’re looking for someone to talk to. You don’t have to handle things alone.
how: An adult you trust: a relative, a teacher, a school counselor, a coach or a friend’s parent. If the first person doesn’t help, tell someone else.
In the US, you can text HOME to 741741 (Crisis Text Line) any time, or call or text Childhelp at 1-800-422-4453. In the UK, call Childline free on 0800 1111.
If you’re thinking about hurting yourself, call or text 988 (US). If you’re in danger right now, call 911 or your local emergency number.

what: After a long shift your body is often still running at work speed, even when you’re home. A short, deliberate wind-down helps it catch up.
how: Two minutes of slow breathing: the Night Garden counts it for you, in the dark and silent by default.
Mark the end of work: change clothes, wash your face, or a short walk round the block.
Write down the one thing still on your mind, so it can wait until tomorrow.
Something low and gentle for the last half hour: calm sounds, no screens with news or messages.
If you’re running on empty most days, the one-minute load check shows how much you’re carrying.

cards.name: a rough patch together

what: I’m sorry. A rough stretch wears you both down, and small things start to land harder than they’re meant.
how: First, look after the next hour: if you’re both still raw, take a proper break and agree when you’ll talk.
When you’re calmer, have a short check-in: one thing that was hard this week, one thing you appreciated, one thing that would help.
If the same argument keeps coming back, “One wants to talk now, one needs space” has a pause plan you can make together.
Then something small and warm: a five-minute moment of turning toward each other, no big talk needed.

cards.name: raising something without it feeling like criticism
cards.pat: \b(tell|say to|bring (it|this|that)? ?up (with|to)|mention (it )?to|raise (it )?with|ask|remind)\b.{0,80}\bwithout (him|her|them|my \w+|it) (feeling|getting|being|sounding|taking it|coming across)\b|\bwithout (sounding|coming across as) (critical|like (i m|im|i am) (nagging|criticis\w+|criticiz\w+|attacking))\b
what: You can say it plainly and kindly at the same time. What makes something land as criticism is usually blame words (“again”, “always”, “never”), talking about the person instead of the thing, and timing, not the fact itself.
how: Pick a calm moment, not the second it happens (unless it’s urgent, like a stove left on: then just say the fact and deal with it).
Say the fact, how it affects you, and one specific ask: “The stove was on when I came in. It scares me. Could we add a stove check to the kitchen close-down?”
Leave out “again”, “always” and “never”. For many people with ADHD those words land on the whole history of being told off.
Make it about a system, not a character: a checklist, a reminder or a habit you both use.
Check the exact words before you send them in “Check a message before you send it”. It keeps your point and shows how it may land.
script: This isn’t a telling-off. The stove was on when I got home and it scared me. Can we work out a check that helps us both?
plain: Pick a calm time.
Say what happened, how you feel, and one ask.
Do not say “again” or “always”.
Fix it with a system, like a checklist.

cards.name: “too sensitive” vs “just being honest”
cards.pat: \b(says|said|thinks|calls me|tells me|told me)\b.{0,10}\b(i m|im|i am|i ve been|i'm)? ?(too|so|over|overly) sensitive\b|\btoo sensitive\b.{0,60}\b(honest|direct|blunt)\b|\b(honest|direct|blunt)\b.{0,60}\btoo sensitive\b|\b(just|only) being honest\b
what: This is usually two styles meeting, not one person being wrong. Some people say things straight and mean no harm; others take in tone and wording as much as the words. “You’re too sensitive” and “you’re too harsh” both put the problem in one person, so neither helps.
how: Name the two styles out loud: “You say things straight. I hear tone strongly. Both are real.”
The direct one keeps the honesty and adds one softener: a warm word first, or “this is about the thing, not you”.
The attuned one asks for the plain meaning when unsure: “Is this a problem, or just information?”
Agree a word either of you can say when something lands harder than it was meant.
Compare your Wave Codes or Wiring Cards: they show this difference side by side, with a bridge for each of you.
script: I don’t want you to stop being honest. I’d like it to land as honest, not harsh. Can we find a way to say hard things that works for both of us?
plain: You have two different styles.
Neither of you is wrong.
Direct talk can add one kind word.
Ask “is this a problem, or just information?”

cards.name: “you don’t do enough” when you feel you do
cards.pat: \b(thinks|says|feels|complains|keeps saying|told me|tells me)( that)? (i|i m|im|i am) (dont|don t|do not|never|not|doesnt|isnt)( do| doing| help| helping| pull| pulling)? ?(enough|my share|anything|much|my weight|my part)\b|\bi do (a lot|lots|loads|more|plenty|stuff|things|so much)\b.{0,40}\b(she|he|they|my \w+) (doesnt|doesn t|does not|dont|don t|never) (see|notice|count|realise|realize)\b
what: Both can be true. You may be doing a lot that isn’t noticed, and your partner may be carrying planning and remembering that you don’t see either. Most of these fights are two people each seeing only their own half.
how: Before you defend, ask: “What’s the part you feel I’m not seeing?” and just listen.

Then each of you writes down what you actually do in a normal week, in your own column. The Lemonade Stand does this, and counts the thinking part (noticing, planning, remembering) as well as the doing.
Your work counts there too: cooking, the car, the bins, whatever it is.
Look at the result together and pick one or two jobs to move, each with one clear owner.
If your partner sent you here, “Sent this by someone?” explains what they can and can’t see.
script: I think I do more than you see, and I bet you do more than I see too. Can we both write it down and look at it together?
plain: You may both be right.

cards.name: how long a break should be
cards.pat: \bhow long (should|do|can|is) (a|the|our|my|we|i)? ?(break|pause|time ?out|cool ?down|cooling off)\b|\bhow long (should|do) (we|i) (take|wait|stay apart|be apart)\b|\b(break|pause|time ?out) (how long|length)\b
what: At least 20 minutes, often 30, and always name a clock time to come back (“back at 8:30”). It takes about that long for a racing heart to settle, so a shorter break usually means picking up where you left off, still flooded.
how: Spend the break calming down (a walk, slow breathing, something absorbing), not rehearsing your case.
Come back at the time you said, even if it’s only to say “I need another half hour.” Keeping the time is what makes a pause feel safe to the other person.
script: I need a break so I don’t say something unfair. I’ll be back at 8:30, and I want to finish this.
links: One wants to talk now, one needs space

plain: Take at least 20 minutes. 30 is often better.
Say a time to come back, like “8:30”.

If you still feel hot, say so and set a new time, rather than pushing through.
If you’re the one who waited: thank them for coming back before you start.

(with me|together)|spend (more )?time (with me|together)|go out (with me|together)|make time for (me|us))\b.{0,60}\b(without it (feeling|being|turning into|becoming) (like )?a chore|without (nagging|begging|forcing|having to ask))\b|\bwithout it (feeling|being) like a chore\b

how: Ask for one clear, small thing. Hints can be easy to miss: “Can we walk together on Sunday morning?” is easier to say yes to than “We never spend time together.”
Keep it small: a walk, a meal, a short drive, a film. Put it in the calendar. Then do it.
Try something new for the two of you now and then. New things together tend to bring back some of the early spark.
Notice and say thank you when they do say yes. That makes the next yes easier.

what: This is one of the most common patterns couples get stuck in, and it belongs to both of you. One of you wants to sort it out now; the other needs time before they can talk well. The more one pushes, the more the other pulls back, and the more one pulls back, the more the other pushes. Neither of you is the problem; the pace mismatch is.
how: If you’re the one who wants to talk now: being walked away from really hurts, and it can feel like being shut out. Ask for a return time rather than an answer right now. A set time is your guarantee the topic isn’t being dropped.

If you’re the one who needs space: a pause is fair, but on its own it can feel like abandonment. Always say when you’ll come back, then come back on time. That’s the hard part, and it’s what makes the pause safe for the other person.
Agree a pause word ahead of time, on a calm day: the word, the shortest break (often 20 minutes or more, until your body has settled), the return time, and the first sentence when you come back.
During the break, calm down rather than rehearse your case. Don’t follow the other person; let the return time do the work.
Nobody is “right” about the pace. You’re both protecting the relationship in your own way.
script: I’m getting flooded and I don’t want to say something unfair. I need a break. I’ll come back at 8:30, and I want to finish this.
I can wait. Can we agree a time? Knowing when we’ll come back helps me let it go for now.

what: Retirement changes a home overnight. Two people who had separate days suddenly share the same rooms and hours, and routines that worked for decades can feel invaded. Re-divide whole jobs rather than “helping”. Owning a job (say, the food shop and meals on Tuesdays) means doing it your way from start to finish, including noticing when it needs doing.
When a job changes hands, agree what “done” means, then let the new owner do it their way. “You’re doing it wrong” is the fastest way to hand the job back.
The partner who has newly retired often needs a purpose outside the house too: a project, volunteering, friends, a regular commitment. That isn’t running away; it gives you both room.

how: When a feeling shows up, ask yourself quietly: is this mine, or am I holding someone else’s?

how: Right now, recovery comes first: somewhere quieter, some water, less light and noise, and no big decisions.
You don’t owe anyone a long explanation today. If you want to say something at work, one short line is enough.
Later, on a calm day, look back at what built up beforehand: noise, a change of plan, too many people, no break, a short night.

what: No, stimming isn’t bad. Rocking, tapping, fidgeting, humming and similar movements are a common way people settle, focus or show joy, and everyone does a little of it.
how: If a stim helps you and doesn’t hurt you or anyone else, there’s no need to stop.
If one causes trouble, like sore skin or a quiet office, you can look for another that does the same job, such as a fidget toy or a quieter movement.
You can add what you do and why to your Wiring Card, so people close to you understand it.

what: Giving more than comes back wears you down, and it isn’t a character flaw. It’s a budget running in the red. The book’s Part One has a section on exactly this: what is in your control, and how to match energy kindly.
how: In your hands: your words, your effort, your rest, your limits, and saying yes, no or “not today.” Theirs to decide: how it lands, whether they change, what they think of you.

cards.name: siblings sharing care for a parent
cards.pat: \b(my )?(brothers?|sisters?|siblings?)\b.{0,40}\b(won t|wont|don t|dont|doesn t|doesnt|never|refuse\w*|barely|hardly)\b.{0,20}\b(help|do|visit|step up|pitch in|share)\w*\b.{0,40}\b(dad|mum|mom|father|mother|parents?|gran|grandma|grandad)\b|\b(share|split|divide)\b.{0,30}\b(looking after|caring for|care (of|for))\b.{0,20}\b(dad|mum|mom|father|mother|parents?)\b.{0,40}\b(brothers?|sisters?|siblings?)\b|\b(get|make) my (brothers?|sisters?|siblings?) (to )?(help|share|step up|do more)\b
what: That’s exhausting, and it’s very common: one sibling ends up as the main carer, often because they live closest or noticed first, and the others “help when they can”. The fair split here is between you and your brothers or sisters, not between you and your parent.
how: Write down what caring for your parent actually involves in a normal week: visits, appointments, medication, paperwork, calls, and the worrying. Seeing it in one place helps the others understand.
Ask each sibling for one specific, ongoing job with a time, rather than “more help”: “Could you take over the insurance calls and phone Dad every Sunday at 6?”
Siblings who live far away can still own things: paperwork, bills, booking appointments, researching care, paying for a sitter.
Talk it through at a planned family call, not in the hallway after an appointment.
Look after yourself too: respite care and carer helplines exist for exactly this.
script: I can’t keep doing most of Dad’s care on my own. Could you each take one thing, like Thursday’s appointment or the Sunday call?
plain: You should not do it all alone.
Write down what the care involves.
Ask each sibling for one clear job.
Get support for yourself too.

cards.name: getting adult children to help with care
cards.pat: \b(my )?(grown |adult )?(daughter|son|kids|children)\b.{0,50}\b(won t|wont|doesn t|doesnt|don t|dont|never|refuses? to)\b.{0,30}\b(help|visit|call|get it|understand)\b.{0,60}\b(dad|mom|mum|father|mother|husband|wife|him|her|caring|care)\b|\b(car(e|ing) for|caregiv\w*|carer|looking after|look after)\b.{0,80}\b(daughter|son|kids|children)\b.{0,30}\b(won t|wont|doesn t|doesnt|don t|dont|never)\b|^(so |and |but )?(how (do |can |should )?i|how to|how do we) ask (my )?(grown |adult |grown up )?(children|kids|son|daughter|sons|daughters)\b.{0,15}\b(for )?(more )?help( (with|caring for|looking after) (him|her|their (dad|mum|mom|father|mother)|my (husband|wife)))?$
what: That’s a lonely place to be. Adult children who live far away often don’t see how much it takes, and many want to help but don’t know what to do. A specific ask usually works better than a general one.
how: Ask for one concrete, regular thing they can do from where they are: a weekly call with their parent at a set time, handling the bills or insurance online, booking appointments, or paying for a sitter one afternoon a week.
Tell them plainly what a normal week looks like for you. People can’t help with a load they can’t see.
If they can visit, ask for a block of time when you can be away, not just a visit when you’re both there.
If they still won’t, that hurts, and it isn’t a reflection of you. Look wider: friends, neighbors, a faith community, paid help and respite care.
script: Could you take over the insurance calls and call Dad every Sunday at 6? That would give me real breathing room.

cards.name: resentment and guilt as a caregiver

what: Resentment and guilt are among the most common feelings caregivers have. They don’t mean you love the person less. They usually mean you’re carrying too much, for too long, with too little rest.
how: Let the feeling be a signal, not a verdict: it’s telling you something needs to change in the setup, not in your heart.
You don’t have to say it to the person you care for. Say it to someone who can hold it: a friend, a support group, a counselor.
Look for one thing to take off your plate this week, even a small one.
If the weight doesn’t lift, or you feel hopeless, please talk to a doctor or counselor. In the US you can call or text 988 any time.

cards.name: making it right with your child after yelling
what: Making it right teaches more than never getting it wrong. Come back once you’ve both calmed down, and go first.
how: Say sorry for the specific thing, without a “but”.
If they were frightened, tell them it wasn’t their fault, and what you’ll change.
Give them a way out next time: “If I start getting loud, you can go to your room, and I’ll come and find you when I’m calm.”
Then keep the promise, and give them a little extra easy time together over the next few days.
script: I scared you when I yelled. That wasn’t okay, and it wasn’t your fault. I’m working on stopping before I get loud.
I’m sorry I yelled. That wasn’t fair to you. Let’s try again.

cards.pat: \bhow (do |can |should )?i stop (yell\w*|scream\w*|shout\w*)\b|\bi (always |keep |constantly |still )?(yell|scream|shout) at (my|the) (kids?|children|son|daughter)\b|\bstop (yelling|screaming|shouting) at (my|the) (kids?|children)\b|\bhow (do )?i stop\b.{0,20}\b(yell\w*|scream\w*)\b
what: Feeling this bad about it means you care, and that matters. Shame tends to make yelling worse, so be as kind to yourself as you’re trying to be to them. Almost every parent yells sometimes. You can change it, and you can repair it when it happens.
how: Notice the warning signs early: a tight jaw, a louder voice, a short fuse. That’s the moment to step back.
Say it out loud: “I’m getting too loud. I’m going to take a breath.” Then breathe slowly for one minute, or step into another room.
Come back and repair: “I’m sorry I yelled. That wasn’t fair to you. Let’s try again.” Kids learn a lot from seeing a grown-up make it right.
Look at what sets it off (being tired, rushed, hungry) and change one thing about that time of day.
script: I’m sorry I yelled. That wasn’t fair to you. Let’s try again.

what: Wanting to message an ex is very common, especially late at night. It usually means you miss them. It doesn’t mean you have to send it.
how: Write it, don’t send it. Type it in your notes, not in your chat with them, and read it again in the morning.
Sleep on it. If you still want to send it after a night’s sleep and a talk with a friend, you’re choosing, not reacting.

Text a friend instead, and mute or archive the chat with your ex so it isn’t the first thing you see. Muting is a kind choice for you, not a statement to them.

what: Yes, it’s common. After a loss, and a breakup is a real loss, feelings tend to come in waves: a hard hour, then an ordinary one. Over weeks, the hard waves usually come less often, and many people recover faster than they expected. As someone on the breakup page put it: “That’s a wave, not a slide.”
how: Keep three basics going: some sleep, a proper meal, and daylight every day.
Once a day, take a one-minute reading of how you are. My weather today keeps it on this device, so you can see the waves get smaller.
Tell one or two people what would help: company, a walk, or a message each evening.
If the heaviness doesn’t lift over a few weeks, if you can’t sleep or eat, or if you feel hopeless, please tell someone today: a friend, your doctor, or a helpline.

what: Crying, weeks or months on, is part of grieving, not a sign you’re stuck. Grieving people tend to swing between facing the loss (remembering, missing them, crying) and getting on with daily life. Both are healthy. A good morning followed by a hard afternoon is not going backwards.
how: There’s no schedule you should be keeping to. The path grief takes varies widely from person to person.
Staying connected to the person who died is healthy: talking to them, keeping a few of their things, marking their birthday.
Enjoying something is not a betrayal of the person you lost.
If the weight doesn’t lift at all over many months, or you can’t manage daily life, talk to your doctor or a grief counsellor. Asking for help doesn’t mean you loved them any less.
plain: Crying is part of grief.
Good and hard hours both come.
There is no timetable.
If it does not lift for months, see a doctor.

cards.pat: \b(my|our) (wife|husband|partner|spouse|mom|mum|mother|dad|father|son|daughter|child|baby|brother|sister|friend|best friend|grandma|grandpa|grandmother|grandfather|dog|cat) (died|passed|passed away|is gone|was killed)\b|\b(lost|losing) (my|our) (wife|husband|partner|spouse|mom|mum|mother|dad|father|son|daughter|child|baby|brother|sister|friend|best friend|dog|cat)\b|\bi m (a )?(widow|widower|widowed)\b|\b(widow|widower|widowed|bereaved|bereavement|grieving|grief|mourning)\b|\bsince (she|he|they) (died|passed)\b
what: I’m so sorry. Losing someone you love changes everything, and there’s no right way or right timetable to grieve. Pulling back for a while is a very common part of it, not a failing.
how: People in the same family often grieve differently: one wants to talk, another keeps busy. Neither is wrong.
Staying connected to the person you lost, through memories and rituals, is healthy. Grief doesn’t have to end in “moving on”.
If you’ve pulled away from family, one small step is enough: a short call, or one honest line like “I’ve been quiet because I miss them, not because of you.”
If the weight doesn’t lift, or you have thoughts of not wanting to be here, please talk to a doctor, a grief counselor, or call or text 988 in the US.

what: Distance with a grown son or daughter is common, especially after a loss or a big change, and it usually isn’t a verdict on you. People grieve and pull back in different ways, and grown children often worry about saying the wrong thing.
how: Start small and regular rather than big: a short call at the same time each week, or one easy invitation, like lunch or help with a small job.
One honest line can open a door: “I’ve been quiet because I miss your mother, not because of you. I’d like to see more of you.”
Let them help you with something practical, like a lift or the new phone. Being useful to you can mean as much to them as it does to you.
If there’s an old hurt between you, say you’d like to hear their side one day, and leave it there for now.

what: It’s hard when time with your friends or family leaves your partner jealous, quiet or sulky afterwards. Feeling jealous is human, and it usually points at something underneath: wanting more time together, or wanting to feel sure of where they stand. It isn’t yours to fix alone, and it isn’t a reason to stop seeing people you care about.
how: Talk about it on a calm day, not as you’re heading out or just back.
Ask what the feeling is about: “What goes on for you when I’m out with them?” Listen before you explain.
Offer what you can, by choice: a text during the evening, a plan for time just the two of you that week, or having them along sometimes.
Keep seeing your friends. Reassurance helps; giving up your people doesn’t, and usually makes the worry bigger.
If you’re ever stopped from seeing people, or you feel afraid of how they’ll react, that’s different, and private help is on the Not safe at home? page.

cards.name: phones, trust and jealousy
cards.pat: \b(fight|fighting|fights|argue|arguing|argument|arguments|row|rows)\w* (about|over) (her|his|their|my|our|the) (phone|phones|texts|instagram|snapchat|tiktok|social media|dms)\b|\b(she|he|they) (s |is |are )?(always |constantly )?on (her|his|their) phone\b|\bjealous\w*\b|\btrust issues\b|\b(she|he|they) (says|said) i (don t|dont|do not) trust (her|him|them)\b|\bi (don t|dont|do not|can t|cant) trust (her|him|them|my (gf|bf|girlfriend|boyfriend|partner|wife|husband))\b
what: Fights about phones are usually about something underneath: feeling left out, worry, or not being sure where you stand. The phone is just where it shows up.
how: Talk about the feeling, not the device: “When you’re on your phone at dinner, I feel like I’m not really there.” That lands better than “you’re always on your phone”.
Agree on one or two simple norms together, like phones away at meals or in bed, rather than one person setting rules for the other.
If it’s about trust or jealousy, say what would help you feel secure, and ask what would help them. Reassurance you both choose works; checking each other’s phones usually makes it worse.
If either of you checks, tracks or controls the other’s phone or friends, that’s a different thing from a disagreement. The Not safe at home? page explains the difference.
script: I don’t want to police your phone. I think what’s really bugging me is feeling a bit shut out. Can we figure out some phone-free time that works for both of us?

cards.name: lonely after a divorce or split
cards.pat: \b(lonely|alone|isolated|so quiet)\b.{0,30}\b(since|after) (the |my |our )?(divorce|split|separation|break ?up|breakup)\b|\b(since|after) (the |my |our )?(divorce|split|separation|break ?up|breakup)\b.{0,30}\b(lonely|alone|isolated)\b
what: Loneliness after a split is very common, especially in the evenings and on weekends without the kids. It’s a signal, a bit like hunger, telling you that you need people. It isn’t a sign that something is wrong with you.
how: Send one easy message today. It doesn’t need to be a big catch-up: “Saw this and thought of you. Fancy a coffee next week?”
Some couple friends may drift, and some will stay. It’s okay to make new ones.
Regular beats big. A weekly thing with the same faces builds friendships faster than one big night out.
If loneliness turns into hopelessness, please talk to someone now: call or text 988 in the US, or Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland.

cards.name: feeling lonely
cards.pat: \b(i feel|i m|im|i am|i ve been|ive been|been|feeling|feel) (so |really |kinda |kind of |pretty |very |a bit |a little |super )?(alone|lonely|isolated)\b|\b(so|really|kinda|very) lonely\b|\bno (one|body) to talk to\b|\bi (don t|dont|do not) have (any )?friends\b
what: That sounds really heavy, and I’m glad you said it. Is it more than a bad day? Feeling lonely is really common, and it isn’t a flaw in you. It’s a signal, a bit like hunger, that you need more connection, and it tends to ease with small, regular contact rather than one big fix.
how: Pick one person and send one easy message today, like “Saw this and thought of you”. Small, low-pressure contact counts.
Put something regular in your week where the same people show up: a class, a club, volunteering, a faith group, or a walk at the same time each day.
Loneliness can make other people seem less friendly than they are. Assume a bit more goodwill than your mind is telling you.

If it’s been heavy for a long time, or you’re feeling hopeless, please talk to a doctor or counselor. If it’s heavier than a bad day, or you feel you can’t go on, please talk to someone now: call or text 988 in the US, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, any time. what: I’m sorry. A breakup is a real loss, even when you wanted it. In the first days the job is small: get through each one. You don’t have to understand what happened yet, or be “over it.”
how: Keep three basics going: some sleep, a proper meal, and daylight every day.
Tell one or two people what has happened, and what would help: company, a walk, or just a message each evening.
Hold off on big decisions you don’t have to make this week.
Go easy on late-night messages to your ex, alcohol, and scrolling their profiles. Muting is a kind choice for you, not a statement to them.
script: We’ve split up. I don’t need advice yet. Could you text me in the evenings this week?
Today I only need to get through today.
plain: A breakup is a real loss.
Sleep, eat and go outside each day.
Tell a friend what would help.
Go easy on late-night texts to your ex.

cards.pat: \b(stuck|caught|torn) (in the middle|between)\b.{0,60}\b(husband|wife|partner|spouse|stepdad|stepmom)\b|\bmy (husband|wife|partner|spouse) is (too )?(strict|harsh|hard|mean|cold) (on|with|to) my (kids|children|son|daughter|teens|teenagers)\b|\bmy (husband|wife|partner) and my (kids|teens|teenagers|children|son|daughter) (don t|dont|do not|can t|cant|won t|wont) get (along|on)\b|\b(husband|wife|partner|boyfriend|girlfriend)\b.{0,40}\b(and )?my (\d+ year old|teen\w*|son|daughter|kids?)\b.{0,40}\b(clash\w*|fight\w*|argu\w*|don t get along)\b|\b(pick|take|choose) (a )?side\b.{0,40}\b(husband|wife|partner|kids?|teen\w*|son|daughter)\b|\b(he|she|my husband|my wife|my partner) thinks i (always )?(take|am taking|m taking) (their|the kids |my kids |her|his) side\b|\b(won t|wont|doesn t|doesnt) (even )?(talk|speak) to (him|her|my husband|my wife|my partner|their stepdad|their stepmom)\b
what: Being in the middle is one of the hardest spots in a blended family. You love your kids, you love your partner, and it can feel like every choice lets one of them down. That’s a very common feeling, and it isn’t a sign you’ve chosen wrong.
how: Meet your partner privately first and agree a few house rules you both stand behind. Then you share them with your kids, so the rules come from their parent.
Ask your partner to lead with warmth for now and leave most discipline to you. That isn’t sidelining them; it’s how stepfamilies usually settle.
Give your partner a real role and say it out loud to the kids, like being in charge of Saturday breakfast or homework help.
Make time just for the two of you, too. A steady couple makes the kids feel safer, not less loved.
script: Can we agree on bedtime and screen rules together tonight? Then I’ll tell the kids, and I’ll back you up when it comes up.

cards.name: feeling like an outsider in a blended family
cards.pat: \b(feel|feels|feeling) like (an outsider|a guest|i don t belong|i dont belong|he doesn t belong|she doesn t belong)\b|\boutsider in (my|our|his|her) own (home|house|family)\b|\bguest in (my|our) own (home|house)\b
what: Feeling like a guest in your own home is very common for stepparents, and for the partner who moved in. It usually eases with time, a clear role, and small shared routines, not by pushing to be accepted faster.
how: Ask for one or two things that are clearly yours in the house, like a job, a routine, or a space, so you’re part of how things run.
Build one regular, low-pressure thing with each stepkid, with no rules attached: a drive, a game, a meal you cook together.
Tell your partner how it feels, without blame: “Sometimes I feel like a visitor here. Could we find a couple of things that are ours?”
Keep your own anchors too: your own kids’ time, your friends, your interests. You don’t have to earn your place by giving everything up.
script: Sometimes I feel like a visitor here. Could we find a couple of things that are ours, and could you back me up on them with the kids?

what: When one parent wants every holiday, a simple, predictable rule usually works better than arguing each year. Check your court order or parenting plan first; it may already say.
how: Alternate the big ones: Thanksgiving with one of you and Christmas with the other this year, then swap next year.
Or split the day: Christmas Eve to noon on Christmas Day with one parent, the rest with the other.
Put it in writing once, with a reply-by date, and keep it the same each year so the kids can count on it.
Teens can say what matters to them, but the adults decide, so they never have to choose.
If they won’t agree to anything, keep messages short and factual, and a mediator or your parenting plan can settle it.

what: Holiday schedules are one of the most common sore spots between separated parents. Your court order or parenting plan comes first; if it covers holidays, that’s the answer, and you can point to it calmly.
how: Check the parenting plan or court order before you write anything. If it’s silent, propose something simple and fair, like alternating years or splitting the day.

Write it short and factual, about the kids and the dates only: “Proposal for Christmas: kids with me Dec 24 to noon Dec 25, with you noon Dec 25 to Dec 26. We swap next year. Can you confirm by Nov 15?”
Don’t tell the kids the plan until both of you have agreed it, so they’re never in the middle.
If you can’t agree, a family mediator or your lawyer can help. Keep copies of what was sent.

cards.name: older kids who want a say in the schedule
cards.pat: \b(kids|teens?|children|son|daughter|they)\b.{0,30}\b(want|wants|asking for|ask for|should get|get) (a|their|any) say\b|\b(should|do|can) (the |our |my )?(kids|teens?|children) (get to )?(choose|decide|pick)\b.{0,30}\b(where|which|who|schedule|holiday|christmas|parent)\b
what: Teens can share their wishes, and it helps to hear them. But the adults make the decision, so no child has to choose between their parents or feel they caused someone’s disappointment.
how: Ask each teen privately and calmly what matters to them (a friend’s party, a family tradition, time with one side), and say clearly: “We’ll decide; we just want to know what matters to you.”
Take their wishes into the conversation with your ex, without quoting them as the reason (“Jaden said he wants…” puts them in the middle).
Check your court order or parenting plan first: it may already set holidays or let older children’s views count.
Tell the kids the plan only once both of you have agreed it, together if you can.
Never ask them to carry messages, report back, or pick a side.
script: We want to hear what matters to you this holiday. Your dad and I will work out the plan, so you don’t have to choose.
plain: Teens can say what they want.
The adults decide.

cards.name: should a stepparent discipline
cards.pat: \bshould i (discipline|punish|tell off|ground|correct|set rules for)\b.{0,40}\b(her|him|them|my step\w*|the kids|his kids|her kids|their kids)\b|\b(discipline|punish|tell off|ground)\w* (my |the |his |her )?step(daughter|son|kids?|children|child)\b|\bstep(dad|mom|mum|parent|father|mother)\b.{0,40}\bdisciplin\w*\b|\bdisciplin\w*\b.{0,40}\bstep(dad|mom|mum|parent|kids?|children|daughter|son)\b|\b(she|he|they|my step\w+)\b.{0,10}\b(flat out |just |completely )?refuses? to (do|listen|follow|clean|help)\b.{0,30}\b(i ask|i say|asked|told)\b
what: Early on, it usually works best when the child’s own parent leads on discipline and the stepparent backs them up. Stepparents build authority through warmth and time first; rules from someone a child doesn’t feel close to yet tend to land as “you’re not my dad”.
how: Agree the house rules with your partner privately first, so you’re saying the same thing.
When you’re in charge alone, act like a trusted babysitter: hold the rules you’ve both agreed (“Your mom and I agreed: phones off at ten”), and leave bigger consequences to their parent.
Tell your partner what happened later, calmly, and let them follow up.
Keep putting in the warm moments: a lift, a joke, a shared show. That’s what lets you hold more of a role later.
Back each other up in front of the kids; disagree in private.
script: Your mom and I agreed the rule is phones off at ten. I’m just holding it while she’s out; she’ll talk to you about anything else.
plain: The child’s own parent leads on rules at first.
Agree the rules together, in private.
Hold the agreed rules when you are in charge.
Build warmth first.

cards.pat: \b(harass\w*)\b.{0,40}\b(my )?(ex|ex wife|ex husband|ex partner|exwife|exhusband|kids dad|kids mom|kids father|kids mother|children s father|children s mother|baby mama|baby daddy|co parent|coparent)\b|\b(my )?(ex|ex wife|ex husband|ex partner|exwife|exhusband|kids dad|kids mom|kids father|kids mother|children s father|children s mother|baby mama|baby daddy|co parent|coparent)\b.{0,60}\b(harass\w*|won t stop (texting|calling|messaging)|texts? me (\d+|dozens|hundreds|thirty|twenty|fifty) times|keeps (texting|calling|messaging) (me )?(all night|every night|nonstop|constantly)|shows up (at my|uninvited)|threaten\w*)\b|\b(keeps|won t stop|wont stop|will not stop) (texting|calling|messaging|ringing)( me)?\b.{0,40}\b(after i (asked|told) (him|her|them) to stop|at all hours|all night|every night|nonstop)\b|\bafter i (asked|told) (him|her|them) to stop (texting|calling|messaging|contacting)\b
what: Repeated messages you’ve asked to stop, messages at all hours, threats about the kids or court, or showing up uninvited can cross the line from conflict into harassment. You don’t have to decide that alone, and you don’t owe an answer to every message.
how: Save everything: screenshots with dates, and keep all contact in one channel, ideally a co-parenting app if your court order allows it.
Reply only about the children and logistics, once a day at a set time, briefly and factually. Silence on everything else is allowed.
Talk to your lawyer or a family-court advocate about what counts as harassment where you live and whether a protective order or a change to the parenting plan fits.
If you’re threatened or feel unsafe, call 911 in an emergency. Advocates at 1-800-799-7233 (or text START to 88788) help people after a separation too, and it’s free and private.

what: With an ex, especially if lawyers are involved, treat every message as something a judge might read one day. Short, factual and about the children is the safest shape.
how: You don’t have to reply tonight. Answer at a set time once a day, and only the parts about the kids or logistics.
Use BIFF: Brief, Informative, Friendly (or at least neutral), Firm. For example: “Got it. I’ll be at the school at 5 on Sunday.”

Skip the history, the feelings and the defending yourself. Don’t admit fault in writing (“It was my fault”, “I always do this”); if something needs owning, say what you’ll do next instead: “I’ll leave earlier on Sundays.”
Keep copies. If messages turn threatening or won’t stop, see the after-separation part of the Not safe at home? page and talk to your lawyer.
script: Thanks for letting me know. I’ll have the kids at the school at 5 on Sunday.

what: That hurts, and it puts your kids in the middle. The best protection is usually steady, calm parenting on your side, not answering it in kind.
how: Don’t criticize your ex back to the kids. Kids feel caught when either parent is put down, and they notice who doesn’t do it.
If they repeat something, keep it short and warm: “I’m sorry you heard that. Grown-up problems are for grown-ups. I love you, and you never have to pick a side.”
Write down specific incidents with dates. If it’s affecting the children, talk to your lawyer, a family mediator, or a child counselor.
Look after yourself too: a friend or counselor who can hear your side means you don’t need the kids to.
