cards.name: how the thirteen fields connect
cards.pat: \b(how|what|which|where|in what way)\b[^?]*\b(fields|areas|subjects|inputs|disciplines|things (you|christian|they) studied|(nine|thirteen|13) (fields|areas|inputs|subjects)|learnings|studies)\b[^?]*\b(connect\w*|link\w*|relate\w*|tie\w*|fit together|overlap\w*|intersect\w*)\b|\bconnections? (between|across|among|in) (the )?(nine|thirteen|9|13|fields|areas|subjects|inputs|disciplines)\b|\b(nine|thirteen|9|13) (fields|areas|inputs|subjects)\b[^?]*\b(connect\w*|link\w*|relate\w*|tie\w*)\b|\bhow (does|do) (it|they|everything|all of (it|this|them)) (all )?(connect|tie together|fit together)\b|\bshow me (the )?(obvious|main|first) connections\b
what: Christian’s thirteen fields (neurobiology, psychology, philosophy, the art of debating, politics, behavioral science, economics, finance, business, holistic therapies, laughter therapy, music, aromatherapy) connect in every one of their 78 possible pairs. I sort them into three layers: 28 obvious, 29 hidden and 21 abstract. There’s also a chain where each field leads logically into the next, all the way round.

They connect along seven kinds of root: balance, signal and noise, feedback loops, limited capacity, ownership and structure, quiet incentives, and state and setting. Here are the 28 most obvious, where two fields share an idea in plain sight:
how: Psychology + Behavioral science (feedback loops): Habits beat willpower, especially when you’re tired. A routine too small to skip keeps going on the bad days. In the program: The 90-second daily check-in (WP-13).
Psychology + Neurobiology (state and setting): How you feel and how your nervous system is running are the same moment, seen from two sides. In the program: Today’s Weather.
Psychology + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Calm the body before the conversation. Words land better once the body has settled. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Philosophy + Business (ownership and structure): “Fair by promises” only works when the promises are written down: one owner per job. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.
Behavioral science + Economics (quiet incentives): People follow what the setup quietly rewards, far more than what they intend. In the program: Pillar V.
Behavioral science + Business (feedback loops): Small, regular reviews catch problems while they’re small, in a company or a home. In the program: What keeps coming back? (WP-04).
Neurobiology + Holistic therapies (limited capacity): A system past its limit can’t think its way back. Settle first, then talk. In the program: Breathe or the Night Garden.

Neurobiology + Aromatherapy (state and setting): What reaches the senses sets the body’s alert level. A noisy room makes every comment arrive louder. In the program: Chapter IV: giving a comment time to land.
Economics + Business (limited capacity): Time and attention get spent like any budget, and they run out like one too. In the program: The Lemonade Stand.
Economics + Finance (balance): Both keep accounts of a limited supply. Together they give the book its ledger and the idea of unbilled debt. In the program: The Preface: unbilled debt.
Finance + Business (ownership and structure): Internal controls give every job an owner and every entry a record. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Holistic therapies + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Both start with the body and the senses, not the argument. In the program: Brain Breakers.

The art of debating + Psychology (signal and noise): Winning an argument and being understood are different goals. Debate trains the first; psychology reminds you the second is why you started talking. In the program: Say it so it lands (WP-09).

The art of debating + Philosophy (signal and noise): Debate grew out of philosophy: a claim is only tested when someone who disagrees gets to push on it. Telling what you know from what you assume is the first move of both. In the program: The Chat analyzer (whole chat).

The art of debating + Politics (ownership and structure): Politics is debate with a decision attached: someone has to hear every side, then decide. A home needs a small version, with each voice heard first and one agreement at the end. In the program: Check-ins.
Politics + Philosophy (ownership and structure): Politics asks philosophy’s questions with real stakes: what is fair, who decides, and who is owed what. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.

Politics + Behavioral science (quiet incentives): Good policy makes the right thing the easy thing: defaults, small rewards, less friction. Good house rules work the same way. In the program: Pillar V.

Politics + Economics (quiet incentives): Politics is largely a contest over who gets limited resources; economics counts them. In a home the resources are time, money and attention. In the program: The Lemonade Stand.

Politics + Business (ownership and structure): Governance means who is accountable for what, how decisions get made, and how to change them. “One owner per job” is governance for a household. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Music + Psychology (state and setting): Music changes mood faster than words, and people use it on purpose: to pump up, to wind down, or to feel less alone. In the program: Drift: calm visualizer.
Music + Neurobiology (state and setting): Rhythm and sound reach the nervous system directly. Slow tempos tend to settle the body and fast ones lift it. In the program: Brain Breakers.

Music + Behavioral science (feedback loops): A song is a loop: a pattern that repeats with small changes. A habit tied to a tune or a time of day is easier to keep. In the program: The 90-second daily check-in (WP-13).

Music + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Music therapy is a recognized form of care: singing, drumming and listening help people settle, feel connected and find words. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Music + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Sound and scent both set the mood of a room before anyone speaks. A playlist in the kitchen does what a candle does. In the program: Brain Breakers.

Music + Laughter therapy (state and setting): Laughter is rhythm too: breath, bounce and sound, in time with other people. A shared laugh and a shared song both say “we’re in step.” In the program: Gentle games (Pause & Play).

Laughter therapy + Psychology (state and setting): A shared laugh tells the body “we’re safe.” Research on couples suggests that gentle humor during a disagreement can help calm it down. In the program: Turning Toward.

Laughter therapy + Neurobiology (state and setting): Laughing is linked with looser muscles and lower stress afterward. It’s a quick way to let the body know the alarm can stand down. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).

Laughter therapy + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Laughter yoga and therapeutic humor are part of the holistic toolkit: a whole-body reset that costs nothing. In the program: The Night Garden.

cards.name: the hidden connections
cards.pat: \b(hidden|less obvious|deeper|surprising|unexpected|subtle|secret|more) connections?\b|\bshow me (the )?hidden( ones)?\b
what: Here are the 29 hidden connections: fields that look far apart until you see the root they share.
how: Psychology + Philosophy (signal and noise): Intent isn’t impact, and most of what’s said in a conflict is a guess wearing the costume of a fact. In the program: The Chat analyzer.
Psychology + Economics (limited capacity): We each remember our own effort best, so unseen work goes uncounted, though it spends real attention. In the program: Who did what (WP-01).

Psychology + Business (ownership and structure): Work with no clear owner lands on whoever notices first, and that person gets called controlling. Unclear ownership turns into hurt feelings. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Psychology + Finance (balance): Goodwill works like a reserve. Thanks and repairs top it up; sharp words draw it down, and a low reserve makes small things feel big. In the program: Turning Toward.

Psychology + Aromatherapy (state and setting): The same sentence lands differently in a calm, quiet room. The setting changes what a person can take in. In the program: Chapter IV: where and when to talk.
Philosophy + Economics (balance): Efficient and fair aren’t the same thing. “It all got done” can hide who quietly did it. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.

Philosophy + Finance (balance): Double-entry bookkeeping is a fairness idea: every entry has two sides, and a book that balances from one side only isn’t balanced. In the program: Your side, their side.

Behavioral science + Neurobiology (limited capacity): A tired body makes good habits harder. That’s why the program’s habits are tiny: they have to survive the worst day of the week. In the program: The 90-second daily check-in (WP-13).

Behavioral science + Finance (quiet incentives): A score you can raise by deleting the hard rows is rewarding the wrong thing. Keep the unowned jobs on the list. In the program: Chapter II: ownership clarity.
Behavioral science + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Cues in a room start habits. A cup of tea or a familiar scent can become your signal to slow down. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).
Neurobiology + Economics (limited capacity): Attention is scarce. Noticing, remembering and planning spend it, even when nobody sees. In the program: The mental load.
Neurobiology + Business (limited capacity): A team past capacity drops things, and so does a body. Both need a safety margin for the ordinary bad week. In the program: Chapter V: a capacity issue.
Neurobiology + Finance (balance): Your battery works like a balance sheet: leftover stress is a debt, and rest is the reserve. In the program: How much are you carrying? (WP-02).
Business + Holistic therapies (feedback loops): Maintenance before breakdown. Care for people the way a good team cares for its systems, before the crisis. In the program: Check-ins.

The art of debating + Behavioral science (feedback loops): Arguments run on habit: the same lines, the same escalation. The best debate trick, restating their point before you answer, only works once it’s practiced enough to be automatic. In the program: The 90-second daily check-in (WP-13).

The art of debating + Economics (quiet incentives): In a debate the reward goes to whoever wins the room. At home the quiet reward for “winning” is the other person giving up, which costs far more than it saves. In the program: Chapter IV: two kinds of fair.

The art of debating + Finance (balance): A good argument keeps honest books: claims on one side, evidence on the other, and no entry without support. “You always…” is a debit with no receipt. In the program: The Chat analyzer (whole chat).

The art of debating + Business (ownership and structure): Good meetings have a chair, an agenda and a decision at the end. A good hard talk at home needs the same: one topic, a turn each, and a named next step. In the program: Check-ins.

The art of debating + Neurobiology (state and setting): Reasoning well needs the thinking part of the brain, and it goes quiet on high alert. The best debate skill is knowing when your body can’t take part yet. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).

The art of debating + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Where an argument happens shapes how it goes. A crowded kitchen at dinnertime argues differently from a quiet walk. In the program: Check-ins: a good moment.

The art of debating + Music (signal and noise): Tone carries more than the words. The same sentence has a pace and a pitch, and spoken softly and slowly it lands differently than spoken fast and flat. In the program: The Chat analyzer.

The art of debating + Laughter therapy (signal and noise): Humor in a disagreement can open a door or slam one. Laughing with someone shows you’re on the same side; laughing at them shuts the talk down. In the program: Say it so it lands (WP-09).

Politics + Psychology (signal and noise): Groups hear what they fear. How a message is framed changes how it’s received, and that’s as true at a dinner table as in a parliament. In the program: The Chat analyzer.

Politics + Finance (balance): A budget is a political document: it shows what a group values. A week’s chores and hours are a household budget, and they show the same thing. In the program: Who did what (WP-01).

Music + Business (ownership and structure): An orchestra works because every player has a part and someone sets the tempo: one owner per job, and one shared beat. In the program: One owner per job (WP-03).
Laughter therapy + Behavioral science (feedback loops): A small, shared bit of silliness gets repeated and sticks. The in-joke is a habit that keeps closeness going. In the program: Turning Toward.

Laughter therapy + Economics (limited capacity): Joy refills what effort spends. A few minutes of play is a cheap way to top up the battery everything else draws on. In the program: Gentle games (Pause & Play).
Laughter therapy + Business (feedback loops): Teams that can laugh together tend to find it easier to say hard things early, while they’re still small. In the program: Check-ins.
Laughter therapy + Aromatherapy (state and setting): A warm, softly lit, relaxed room makes laughter easier. The senses set the mood for play as much as for calm. In the program: Brain Breakers.

cards.name: the abstract connections
cards.pat: \b(abstract|philosophical|big picture|underlying|universal|most abstract) connections?\b|\bshow me (the )?abstract( ones)?\b
what: Here are the 21 abstract connections: the deepest patterns, where the fields stop looking like separate subjects at all.
how: Philosophy + Behavioral science (feedback loops): Aristotle thought we become what we repeatedly do. Character, like a habit, is built by small acts, not by one big decision. In the program: Small and often.
Philosophy + Neurobiology (state and setting): If shutting down or getting revved up is a body doing its job, it isn’t a character flaw. That changes what blame means. In the program: Pillar II.

Philosophy + Holistic therapies (balance): A setup can be sustainable without being good for the people in it. Asking what makes the whole person well is a different question from “does it work?” In the program: Chapter II: what the number is not.

Philosophy + Aromatherapy (state and setting): What we take in through the senses shapes what we believe is true. Two people in one room may not be perceiving the same room. In the program: See it from their side (Rewind the talk).

Behavioral science + Holistic therapies (feedback loops): The smallest repeated acts, a breath, a daily check-in, a weekly look back, are rhythms, and rhythm is how a body and a relationship stay in tune. In the program: Chapter V: the rhythms.

Economics + Holistic therapies (balance): Rest isn’t time lost. It keeps the capacity that everything else spends, so skipping it is borrowing against next week. In the program: Wavelength: what fills you up.

Economics + Aromatherapy (quiet incentives): A room, like a market, carries costs nobody pays out loud. A rushed, noisy setting quietly taxes every conversation in it. In the program: Chapter IV: the setting.

Business + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Good workplaces are designed so the setting helps people do their best. A home can be too: a quiet corner for hard talks is a design choice. In the program: Check-ins: a good moment.

Finance + Holistic therapies (balance): A setup score says whether an arrangement can last, never whether it’s worthwhile. Holistic care asks the other question: what makes the whole person well. In the program: Chapter II.

Finance + Aromatherapy (balance): Changing the setting costs almost nothing and pays back on every conversation held there: the cheapest investment in the whole program. In the program: Chapter IV: where and when to talk.

The art of debating + Holistic therapies (state and setting): Holistic care treats the whole person, and so does a good debate partner. The person across from you is tired, hungry or hurt as well as holding a position. In the program: See it from their side (Rewind the talk).

Politics + Neurobiology (state and setting): The nervous system treats a threat to “our side” as a threat to the self. Calm bodies compromise more, which is why settling comes before the vote. In the program: The Calm-Down Kit (WP-11).

Politics + Holistic therapies (balance): Public health and holistic care agree that wellbeing is shaped by the conditions around a person, not only by their choices. Fix the conditions. In the program: Pillar II.

Politics + Aromatherapy (state and setting): Politics knows the setting is a message: where the table is, how the room is laid out, who sits where. A home can use the same craft for hard talks. In the program: Check-ins: a good moment.
Politics + Music (feedback loops): Anthems and marching songs show how music binds a group. A shared beat is how a crowd starts to feel like one body. In the program: The theme song music video.

Politics + Laughter therapy (signal and noise): Groups have long used jokes and satire to say what can’t be said straight about power. At home, a light touch lets a sore topic be raised, if both people are in on the joke. In the program: Check-ins.
Music + Philosophy (balance): Thinkers since Pythagoras have asked why sound moves us. Harmony is a picture of fairness: different parts, each with room, in one piece. In the program: Echoes of Gold.
Music + Economics (limited capacity): Attention is what a song and a market both compete for, and it runs out. A noisy setting taxes every conversation held in it. In the program: Brain Breakers.

Music + Finance (balance): In music a rest is written into the score, and silence counts as much as sound. In a household the quiet work needs writing down too. In the program: The Preface: unbilled debt.

Laughter therapy + Philosophy (signal and noise): Thinkers have long said humor spots what’s out of place: the gap between how things are and how they should be. A good joke names the gap without blaming anyone. In the program: See it from their side (Rewind the talk).

Laughter therapy + Finance (balance): Goodwill is a reserve, and shared laughs are deposits that don’t appear on any sheet but make the withdrawals of a hard week survivable. In the program: Turning Toward.

cards.name: How you connect (Wavelength)
cards.what: Wavelength is a free guide to how you think, how you communicate and how you take things in, both giving and receiving. It replaces Your Heartprint (the old Heartprint page now opens Wavelength, and saved Heartprint answers move over). You pick your wiring if you like (any mix, or none), tap through four short parts with either/or questions and statements common for your wiring, choose the 9 inputs of learning that help you, and pick what helps you feel understood. You get a four-letter Wave Code and one of 16 archetypes, like the Firefly, with what each letter means, its gift and how to tune in. Then there are sixteen self-discovery chapters, a page on how the 9 inputs connect, an optional personal statement, and a way to compare codes with someone. It’s a fun way to describe preferences, not a diagnosis or a test that measures you. Nothing you type or choose is sent anywhere.
how: Open Wavelength, add your first name if you like, and tap Start.
Pick your wiring (optional, select all that apply), or use the “Not sure which fits?” guide.

Answer the four parts: how your brain gets going (pace), how you think things through (lens), how you communicate out (sending) and how you take things in (receiving). Tap any statements that sound like you.
Choose your inputs of learning and your strongest, then what helps you feel understood.
Part 7, your statement, is optional: the old Heartprint steps, with “Things you might not have noticed.” Skip it if you like.
Read your Wave Code, open the chapters, explore how the 9 inputs connect, and compare with someone. Copy my profile and Copy my journal are on your results.
cards.results: Your results show your four letters (Q or S for pace, F or T for lens, D or N for sending, E or A for receiving), your archetype, how strongly you lean on each line, and a waveform drawn from your code: faster waves for Quick Spark, sharp edges for Trees, taller for Direct, echoes for Attuned. Each letter opens to what it means, its gift, what to watch for and how someone can tune in to you. It’s a description of preferences, not a verdict or a diagnosis, and everyone uses both ends of each line sometimes.
cards.more: Privacy: everything happens in your browser. Your answers and journal are kept on this device only if you tick “Keep my answers and journal on this device,” and “Erase everything” on your results removes them. The statement part is the old Your Heartprint: nine quick steps (what’s going on now, how you’re wired, what fills you up, what drains you, what people notice when you’re stretched, what helps, how you show care, the unseen work you do and what matters most) that write a warm note you can copy, save or print.
cards.ex: Say Sam answers quickly and thinks out loud (Q), wants the big picture first (F), cushions hard things (N) and reads tone closely (A). Sam is QFNA, the Firefly: bright, warm, full of ideas and quick to sense how others feel. Sam’s partner is STDE, the Compass. Comparing shows four different letters, so they agree on a few things: Sam labels brainstorms, the partner says “I’ll come back to you by tonight,” they start with the why and then the first step, and they agree that plain words aren’t anger.

cards.name: the deepest connections, where many fields meet
cards.pat: \b(deepest|most hidden|deeper still|even deeper)\b[^?]*\b(connection|connections|link|links|fields?|ones?)\b|\bwhere\b[^?]*\b(all|nine|thirteen|9|13|the|many) (nine |thirteen |9 |13 )?(fields|subjects|areas)?\s?(all )?meet\b|\bintersection of (all|the nine|the thirteen|the 9|the 13)\b|\b(all|nine|thirteen|9|13) (fields )?(meet )?at once\b
what: Past obvious, hidden and abstract, there's a deepest level: moments where many of the thirteen fields meet at once. Here are 6:
how: One hard conversation, all thirteen fields at once (13 fields: Neurobiology, Psychology, Philosophy, The art of debating, Politics, Behavioral science, Economics, Finance, Business, Holistic therapies, Laughter therapy, Music, Aromatherapy). A single tense talk about the dishes runs through every field in the program, one after another, in a few seconds. Then you decide: talk now, or name a better time. Either way, you’re choosing with the whole picture.

The job nobody owns (6 fields: Psychology, Behavioral science, Economics, Finance, Business, Philosophy). Each of us remembers our own effort best (psychology). A job with no owner drifts to whoever notices first (behavioral science). Noticing spends real attention (economics), so a debt builds up that nobody writes down (finance). Business calls it a missing owner. Philosophy calls it unfair. They’re all describing the same unwritten job.

The tired week (6 fields: Neurobiology, Holistic therapies, Behavioral science, Economics, Finance, Business). A worn-out body has less to give (neurobiology), so rest has to match effort (holistic therapies). Habits have to be small enough to survive that week (behavioral science). A household running at full stretch has no safety margin (economics) and no reserve for a surprise (finance), and a team in the same state drops things (business). One tired week shows that capacity is a single root under six fields.

The room does some of the talking (6 fields: Aromatherapy, Neurobiology, Psychology, Philosophy, Economics, Business). Noise, light and smell reach the senses first (aromatherapy and the senses) and set the body’s alert level (neurobiology). That changes what a person can take in (psychology), and even what they believe happened (philosophy). A rushed, noisy room quietly taxes every conversation in it (economics), and good workplaces are designed to avoid that (business). Choosing the place is part of the conversation.

Making a house rule (5 fields: Philosophy, The art of debating, Politics, Business, Behavioral science). Agreeing on a rule is politics at the smallest scale. Philosophy asks what is fair. Debate says each side should be able to state the other’s case before answering. Politics is how a group decides, and who gets a say. Business gives the rule an owner, and behavioral science makes it easy enough to follow on a bad day.

The mood of the room (5 fields: Music, Laughter therapy, Aromatherapy, Neurobiology, Holistic therapies). Sound, a shared laugh and the setting reach the body before any words do. Music sets the tempo (music), a laugh lets the body stand down (laughter), and light, scent and noise set the mood of the room (aromatherapy and the senses). Neurobiology explains why it works, and holistic care says to start there.
cards.pillar: These are the whole program in one moment: read your state, check what you know, count the load, give the job an owner, and mind the setting.

cards.name: the chain through all thirteen fields
cards.pat: \b(how|does|do)\b[^?]*\b(one|each) (field|subject|area)\b[^?]*\b(lead|leads|flow|flows|follow|follows) (in)?to\b|\b(the )?chain (of|through|across)? ?(the )?(nine|thirteen|9|13|all|fields)?\b|\bshow me the chain\b|\bhow one field leads into the next\b
what: The thirteen fields also line up in a chain, where each one follows logically from the last, and the last leads back to the first. Read it as one argument:
how: Neurobiology → Psychology: The body’s state comes first. It shapes what you feel, and how every word you hear lands.
Psychology → Philosophy: Once you know feelings color what you hear, you have to ask what you actually know, and what you’re only assuming.
Philosophy → The art of debating: Knowing what’s fair isn’t enough. You have to be able to say it, and to test it with someone who disagrees, without it turning into a fight.
The art of debating → Politics: Debate between two people becomes politics when a group has to decide: who gets a say, who chooses, and how a disagreement ends without a loser.
Politics → Behavioral science: Fair rules agreed on aren’t enough. Good intentions fade under stress, so you need habits and structures that work on bad days.
Behavioral science → Economics: Structures run on incentives. People follow what the setup rewards, and every choice spends a limited supply of time and attention.
Economics → Finance: If time and attention are limited, they can be counted: a ledger of who spends what, the unseen work included.
Finance → Business: Counting isn’t enough on its own. Each regular job needs an owner and a simple check, or the books drift again.
Business → Holistic therapies: Systems are run by people. A team, or a home, only works if the people in it are cared for, not just managed.
Holistic therapies → Laughter therapy: Caring for the whole person includes joy. A shared laugh is a reset for the body and a repair for the relationship, and it costs nothing.
Laughter therapy → Music: Laughter and music do the same quiet work: they bring people into step, with a shared breath and a shared beat.
Music → Aromatherapy: Sound is one of the senses that sets the mood of a room, along with light and scent, and the setting is part of every conversation.
Aromatherapy → Neurobiology: And the senses feed straight back into the nervous system, setting the body’s state, which is where the chain began.
cards.pillar: Each step is a pillar in action. Together they’re the program in one loop: read your state, check what you know, argue kindly, decide fairly, build habits, count the load, give jobs owners, care for the people, share a laugh, find the beat, and mind the setting.

cards.name: See their side (a step of Rewind the talk)
cards.what: See it from their side is now the “See their side” step of Rewind the talk (the Carrier Wave Decoder). Once it was its own page, the Perspective Shifter. It helps you see a moment from the other person’s side. You tap what might be true for them: who they are to you, the state they were in, what was going on around them, how they’re wired and what history they carry. Then you note what each of you could and couldn’t see. It builds a picture of how the moment may have looked to them, why it can look different from what was meant, questions to check instead of guessing, and a sentence to bridge the gap that you can test in the Chat analyzer.

Tap what might be true for them in each group. Their side builds itself as you go.
Look closely at “What could each of you see?”: most misunderstandings come from different information, not different values.
Use the questions to check, and test the bridge sentence in the Chat analyzer before you say it.

cards.name: the page for grandparents
cards.what: The page for grandparents is for anyone who helps with the grandkids: grandparents, great-aunts and great-uncles, and other older relatives who often care for children in the family. It shows how to check your own tank before a busy visit, share the load fairly so help doesn’t quietly turn into an unspoken full-time job, agree on house rules with your grown children (their house, their rules; your house, a few gentle ones you agree on), say no kindly, be a calm place for the grandkids and stay close from far away.
how: Before a busy visit, take one minute with Today’s Weather to see how full your own tank is.
Write down every job you do for the grandkids in a normal week, and give each regular one an owner with One owner per job (WP-03).
Ask the parents for their top three rules (screens, sweets, bedtime) and keep to those. Everything else can be your own way at your house.
Say plainly when you can help and for how long: “I can do Tuesdays and Thursdays until five.” A clear yes is easier to keep than a vague always.
For calm time together, watch a chapter of Frequency Buddies or play the Night Garden, side by side or on a call.
cards.ex: Ruth looked after her grandsons three days a week and felt hurt when her daughter said she spoiled them. Over a cup of tea, her daughter named one thing: candy after school. Ruth swapped it for fruit and a story, and kept her own ways for everything else.

cards.name: the Complacency guide
cards.what: Complacency is what happens when something has worked for a long time and you stop checking on it. It isn’t laziness or a lack of love. It’s a setup nobody has looked at lately. The Complacency guide covers the quiet signs, how it shows up in you, partners, family, friends, housemates and coworkers, how it differs from contentment and acceptance, and small, regular re-checks.
how: Notice the quiet signs: “fine” is the whole conversation, thanks has become a reflex, “we’ve always done it this way” is the reason.
Ask one real question you don’t already know the answer to, and listen to all of it.
Say one specific thank-you a week.
Put a small re-check on the calendar: daily 90-second check-in, weekly question and thanks, monthly look-back, quarterly “does this still work for everyone?”
Keep it light: a re-check is a look, not a trial.
cards.pillar: Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives, and Pillar I, See the whole load.

cards.name: the Re-check Drive
cards.what: The Re-check Drive is a calm football game made from the complacency playbook. You pick who it’s for (yourself or someone close), call a play like “ask a question you don’t know the answer to,” do it for real, and tell the game you did. Each one moves the ball toward a field goal. There’s no clock, no opponent that can score, and no way to lose.
how: Pick who the drive is for, then tap Start the drive.
Call a play from your hand, do it in real life, and tap “I did it.” “Not today” costs nothing.
Share your own context and ask for theirs: both sides’ context is part of a good drive.
When you reach field-goal range, kick it. Your drive is saved only in your browser.
cards.pillar: Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives, with Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: touchstones
cards.what: A touchstone is a small, shared piece of language or meaning that says “we’re us”: an inside joke, a pet name, the way you say hello, a song, a place or a story you retell. A few words carry a whole history. They can go stale when they’re said on autopilot, and they’re one of the quickest ways to bring warmth back. There is now a whole guide to them, written like the love languages guide, with a short list you can fill in.
how: Retell a story from both sides: how you met, or how a joke began.
Say an old phrase or pet name on purpose, and see if it still lands.
Agree plain words for hard moments in advance, like a weather word (“my sky is clear, gusty or fogged in”) or a pause word (“pause, back at eight”).
Retire any nickname or joke that hurts, and ask before assuming the words are shared.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, and Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives.

cards.name: the Upset right now page
cards.pat: \b(we re|we are|were|i m|i am|im) (in|having|having a|in a|right in the middle of( a)?) (a )?(fight|argument|row|blowup|blow up|shouting match)( right now| now)?\b|\b(fighting|arguing|yelling|shouting) (right now|at the moment|as we speak)\b|\b(right now|at the moment)\b[^?]*\b(fighting|fight|argument|arguing|both upset|so upset|so angry)\b|\bwe re both (upset|angry|mad|yelling|worked up)\b|\bboth (of us )?(upset|angry|worked up|yelling)\b[^?]*\b(what|how) (do|should|can) (we|i)\b
what: Here is a five-minute way through, for two upset people. Nothing is saved, and it works on one phone.
how: Say a pause line with a return time: “I want to get this right and I’m too worked up. Can we pick this up at eight?”
Breathe out longer than you breathe in: in for 4, out for 6, for about a minute.
Move apart for at least twenty minutes. Drink water, walk, and don’t rehearse the argument.
Come back on time: “I’m back. The topic is still the sink. I am not against you.”
Say back what you heard, then say yours in three parts: a fact, a feeling and one small ask.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

Rewind the talk (the Carrier Wave Decoder)

cards.name: the New baby page
cards.what: A new baby adds a job nobody can see: keeping track of everything. When you are both tired, it lands on whoever notices first. The New baby page gives three small steps to keep that from landing on one of you by accident, and a note on when sad or anxious feelings are worth telling a doctor about.
how: List every job, including the thinking part: the pediatrician visits, noticing the diapers are low, meals, the family chat, thank-you notes.
Give each job one owner. That person does it and also remembers it.
Review it once a week for ten minutes: what felt heavy, and one job to swap.
If sadness or anxiety lasts more than two weeks or gets heavier, tell a doctor or nurse. In the US, Postpartum Support International’s helpline is 1-800-944-4773.
cards.pillar: Pillar I, See the whole load.
links: Invisible labor and the mental load

cards.name: the Separated co-parents page
cards.what: After a separation, the goal is calm, brief, child-focused contact. The Separated co-parents page has an exchange-day script, ways to keep kids out of the middle, a tone check, and a parallel-parenting route for a co-parent who won’t cooperate. A court order or parenting plan always comes first, and it is not legal advice.
how: Keep it short and about the child: “Hi. Homework’s done. Pick-up is Sunday at five.”
Never use the kids as messengers. Send messages to the adult.
Give each task one owner, in a shared calendar or a short note.
Park bigger things: “Can we put that on Thursday’s check-in?”

If the other parent frightens you, or tries to control where you go or who you see, put your safety first: plan exchanges in public or through a third person, and keep your messages short and factual.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.

cards.name: Share the load, step by step
cards.what: There are several tools for splitting the load, and they work best in an order. Most households only need the first three.
how: Name every job, including the thinking part, with the fair chore chart.
See the split in plain numbers with the Lemonade Stand.
Give each job one owner with One owner per job.
Look back each week, and monthly with What keeps coming back?
cards.pillar: Pillar I, See the whole load.
links: Share the load, step by step

cards.name: Method and limits
cards.what: Every score on the site is written out on one page: how it is worked out, where the cut-offs are, and what it can’t tell you. The rules are simple and chosen by hand, not fitted to data, and none of them predicts anything.
how: The stress check adds five questions scored 0 to 4 and divides by 20.
The Lemonade Stand describes each person’s share of the hours, with words chosen at 60% and 90% for two people.
The setup check weights balance, ownership and stress at 0.40, 0.35 and 0.25.

cards.name: the Love languages guide
cards.what: The five love languages (words, acts of service, gifts, quality time and touch) are a friendly way to talk about how people give and feel care. Research does not support one fixed language per person, so the guide treats them as a menu, with what is healthy and unhealthy about each, how to practice, how to talk about it, and similar ideas such as apology languages, bids for connection and responsiveness.
how: Remember three real moments you felt most cared for, and share them.
Tick what would feel like care right now on the care card, and swap cards.
Offer one thing from the other person’s card each week, and ask for one from yours.
Ask in your weekly review: “What made you feel most cared for this week?”
If someone uses “love” to control you, that is not a language mismatch. Put your safety first.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, and Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives.
links: Love languages: a menu, not a label

cards.name: See and feel the sound
cards.what: See and feel the sound is the big stage at the top of the Soundscapes page. It draws the Brain Breaker that is playing as a large live picture (stars, aurora, rings, tunnel, bars or wave, or Auto, which picks looks that suit the track), with a live card showing the track’s own notes and an energy meter, can go full screen, and a slim bar follows you down the page while something plays. On an Android phone with Chrome it can also vibrate gently with the sound: a pattern that matches the track, a rumble that follows the low tones, a beat, or a steady heartbeat. Vibration is off until you choose a strength. iPhones can’t vibrate from a web page, so there you can see the sound and feel it through the speaker or headphones.
how: Open Soundscapes. The big stage is at the top.
Press See and feel this on a track, or press play on one.
Pick a look: Auto, Stars, Aurora, Rings, Tunnel, Bars or Wave. Try Full screen. With reduced motion on, you get a still, slowly changing glow.
On an Android phone, choose Soft, Medium or Strong under Feel, then pick Match the track, Rumble, Beat or Heartbeat. Try a pulse first.
The Upset right now page can also buzz in time with its breathing pacer.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: Brain Breakers and Brain Breaks
cards.what: Brain Breakers are four instrumental pieces by Christian’s Lab, from soft to cinematic, on the Soundscapes page, made for a short break between program steps: come get your brain wrecked, broken in a good way. A Brain Break card sits at the top of the home page and at the end of each program page. Press a button, take about three minutes, and the card then offers the next step in the program. Nothing plays until you press a button, and the only thing kept is a count of breaks on your own device.
how: Press one of the four tracks on the home page or at the end of a chapter or worksheet, or press Surprise me.
Keep your eyes off the screen if you like. It is about three minutes.
When it ends, follow the link to the next step in the program.
Want more? The Brain Breakers section on Soundscapes has all four tracks, with notes on what each is best for, and See and feel the sound draws and vibrates with them.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: Find your Brain Breaker
cards.what: Find your Brain Breaker is a short picker on the Soundscapes page. Tap what you need (quiet a busy mind, calm anxious energy, wind down before sleep, recover with a spark, get curious and alert, get unstuck, a walk or light planning, or feel something big), how your body is, and how you like sound, and it suggests one of the four tracks with the reasons, plus the other two. You can save a go-to for each need, and it shows what you play most. All of that stays on your device.
how: Open Soundscapes and find Find your Brain Breaker near the top.
Tap what you need right now. Add how your body is, and how you like sound, if you want.
Press Play it, or try one of the others.
Save a go-to if one works for you. Bigger sounds can feel like too much when you are overwhelmed, so the picker leans toward Shooting Star then.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.

cards.name: how the book is arranged
keys: where should i start the book
is there a part about myself
is there a chapter about me
part of the book about myself
how is the book laid out
cards.what: The book now starts with you. Part One, “The most important: yourself,” has three short sections: Then (where your lens came from), Now (your wiring, your weather and your words) and Next (what matters to you, one small goal, tiny steps and a kind monthly look at yourself). Part Two, “Between us,” is the Preface and Chapters I to V on sharing the work, talking, fairness and the monthly look-back. Part Three, “Keeping it warm,” is a reading list of guides: love languages, complacency, turning toward and check-ins. You can read in any order, and each page has a short version and a full one.
how: Start with Then if you like to begin at the beginning, or Now if you want to read yourself first.
Take Next when you want to choose one small thing to grow toward.
When you are ready to bring someone else in, move on to the Preface and Chapter I.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first.
links: Introduction: how the book is laid out

cards.name: apology languages
keys: how do i apologise so it lands
how do i apologize so it lands
how do i say sorry so it lands
cards.what: Apology languages are five parts of a sorry that different people need: expressing regret, accepting responsibility, making it right, a plan to change, and asking for forgiveness (Chapman and Thomas). The idea is popular and little tested, so the page treats it as a menu. The better-supported finding is that acknowledging responsibility and offering to repair matter most. The guide has healthy and sideways versions of each, scripts, and a way to ask “what helps you most after a hurt?” on a calm day.
how: Ask on a calm day: “When I’ve upset you, what helps most: hearing sorry, hearing I understand, or seeing me fix it?”
Say it in three parts: what happened, that it was yours, and one thing you will do.
Check afterwards: “Did that cover it, or is there a part I missed?”
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, and Pillar II, Fix the setup, not the person.

cards.name: appreciation at work
keys: appreciation to my team at work
cards.what: Appreciation at work is the workplace version of love languages (Chapman and White): words, quality time, acts of service, small gifts and appropriate touch like a handshake. It is popular and little tested, so the page uses it as a menu and a question to ask: how do you like to be thanked? The sturdier advice is to be specific, timely, sincere and fitted to the person, and never to use thanks in place of fair pay, workload or credit.
how: Ask a coworker: “When something goes well, what is a way of saying thanks that you actually like?”
Say what they did and what it made possible.
Once a month ask yourself whom you have not thanked in a while.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive, and Pillar V, Notice the quiet incentives.

cards.name: how the languages fit together
keys: how do love languages and apology languages fit
cards.what: The languages of connection page puts it all in one picture: six layers from you outward. First you (self-discovery), then how you talk and listen (Wavelength and the Wiring Card), how you show care (love languages), the words you share (touchstones), how you repair (apology languages), and how you keep it alive (turning toward, check-ins and the complacency re-checks). It has a table of what to reach for in each situation, how well each idea holds up, and a worked example.
how: Find the row in the table that sounds most like this week.
Read that one page and try one small thing from it.
If you only do one thing, start with yourself.
cards.pillar: Pillar IV, Tune how you send and receive.
links: Stay close: our shared words and rituals (Touchstones)

cards.name: your part, and matching energy
keys: only do what i can control
i give more than i get
cards.what: A thread through the whole book: you can only do what’s in your control, and you protect your own energy by matching energy with energy. In your hands: your words, your effort, your rest, your limits and what you ask for. Not yours: someone else’s mood, reply, pace or choices. Matching energy means giving in proportion to what comes back: warmth for warmth, effort for effort, and a little less when you keep giving far more than you get. It’s about care and effort, never volume or punishment, and in a hard season you match someone’s capacity, not their output.
how: Notice where you’re giving far more than comes back.
Name it once, without blame: “I’ve noticed I’m usually the one who plans. I’d love it if you started the next one.”
Adjust your side, kindly, and see what comes back.
Keep giving fully to children and anyone who depends on you, and choose on purpose when to carry more for a season.
cards.pillar: Pillar III, Read your state first: your battery is the budget you’re protecting.
links: Part One: who you are today

cards.name: a sad or heavy day
cards.pat: \b(i|im|i m|i am) (feel|feeling|am feeling|m feeling)? ?(so |really |very |a bit |kind of |kinda )?(sad|low|blue|miserable|hopeless|empty)( today| tonight| lately| right now| again)?$|^(im|i m|i am|feeling) (so |really |very |a bit )?(sad|miserable|hopeless)\b|\b(tired|sick|exhausted) of (everything|it all|life|all of it)\b|\b(having|had) (a|such a) (bad|awful|horrible|rough|terrible|sad) day\b|\bnothing (feels|seems) (worth it|good anymore)\b|\b(low|down|sad|empty|flat) and (alone|lonely)\b|\b(alone|lonely) and (low|down|sad|empty)\b|^(i feel like )?(nobody|no one|noone) (really )?(gets|understands|gets|cares about|listens to|likes) me\b|\bi (feel|m|am) (like )?(nobody|no one|noone) (really )?(gets|understands|cares about) me\b|^(i|im|i m|i am) (feel|feeling|am feeling|m feeling)? ?(so |really |very |pretty |kind of |kinda )?(low|down)\b
what: That sounds really heavy. Is it more than a bad day? Either way, you don’t need a reason, or to have it all worked out, to deserve some kindness.
how: Start with your body: a glass of water, something to eat, a few slow breaths, or a short walk outside.
Tell one person you trust, even in one line: “I’m having a hard day.”
Make the day smaller: pick one small thing to do, and let the rest wait.
If you feel this way most days for more than two weeks, or it’s hard to get through the day, talk to your doctor. That’s a normal, sensible step.

If it’s heavier than a bad day, or you feel you can’t go on, please talk to someone now: call or text 988 in the US, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, any time. Under 18 in the UK? Childline is free on 0800 1111, or text SHOUT to 85258.
script: I’m having a hard day. I don’t need you to fix it. Could you just keep me company for a bit?
plain: I’m sorry you feel this way.
Drink some water and eat something.
Tell one person you trust.
If it lasts more than two weeks, see your doctor.
If you feel you can’t go on, call or text 988 (US) or 116 123 (UK). Under 18 in the UK: Childline, 0800 1111.

cards.name: how feelings work (Part Three, chapter 1)
cards.what: Chapter 1 of Part Three, “Understanding people”, explains how feelings work: they start as signals in the body, naming a feeling helps it settle a little, and we often have feelings about our feelings. It ends with kind words to use on your own, at home, with friends and at work.
how: Notice where the feeling sits in your body first.
Put it into a word or two: “I’m feeling tense.” Naming it helps.
Ask what it is asking for: rest, help, a boundary, comfort.
Read the in-depth version for the research and exercises.

cards.name: stress and the nervous system (Part Three, chapter 2)
cards.what: Chapter 2 of Part Three explains how stress works: your body getting ready, the calm, revved up and running on empty ladder, flooding, why stress adds up, and the kinds of rest that help you recover.
how: Check where you are on the ladder: calm, revved up, or running on empty.
If you are flooded, pause first and talk later.
Pick the kind of rest that fits: sleep, quiet, movement, or company.
links: Chapter 2: Stress and the nervous system

cards.name: how we see each other (Part Three, chapter 3)
keys: how do we see each other
why do we assume the worst
why do i see things differently
why do we see things differently
why do we see things so differently
why do people see things differently
cards.what: Chapter 3 of Part Three is about how we see each other: perception is a best guess, we fill gaps with stories, everyday bias creeps in, and asking beats guessing.
how: Notice the story you are telling about why they did it.
Ask one curious question before deciding what it meant.
links: Chapter 3: How we see each other

cards.name: how communication works (Part Three, chapter 4)
keys: why do we misunderstand each other
cards.what: Chapter 4 of Part Three explains how communication works: meaning is made between two people, so listening, checking and repairing mix-ups matter as much as the words.
how: Say one thing at a time, then check: “What did you hear me say?”
Repair mix-ups early and lightly.

cards.name: attachment, trust and belonging (Part Three, chapter 5)
keys: why do we need to belong
cards.what: Chapter 5 of Part Three is about attachment, trust and belonging: why belonging is a basic need, how early bonds shape what we expect, how trust grows in small moments, and how to rebuild it.
how: Trust grows from small promises kept.
Look for one place where the same people show up each week.

cards.name: habits and change (Part Three, chapter 6)
keys: how do i change a habit
cards.what: Chapter 6 of Part Three is about habits and change: why change is hard, how habits run on cues, and how tiny steps, a kinder setup and self-compassion after slips help change last.
how: Make the step tiny and tie it to something you already do.
Change the setup, not just your willpower.
After a slip, be kind and start again the next day.

cards.name: self-worth, shame and self-compassion (Part Three, chapter 7)
cards.what: Chapter 7 of Part Three is about self-worth, shame and self-compassion: worth is not a score, shame is different from guilt, and self-compassion helps you own mistakes and grow.
how: Guilt says “I did a bad thing”; shame says “I am bad”. Aim for the first.
Talk to yourself the way you would talk to a friend.

cards.name: loss, grief and big life changes (Part Three, chapter 8)
cards.what: Chapter 8 of Part Three is about loss, grief and big life changes: grief comes in waves, not neat stages, it lives in the body, some losses nobody sees, and you can stay connected to who you lost.
how: Expect waves, not a straight line.
Name the losses nobody else sees, too.
links: Chapter 8: Loss, grief and big life changes

cards.name: minds that work differently (Part Three, chapter 9)
cards.what: Chapter 9 of Part Three is a plain guide to neurodiversity: autism, ADHD, sensory and learning differences, masking and energy, and how to meet in the middle at home and at work.
how: Different is not broken: ask what helps, rather than guessing.
Masking costs energy; plan rest after it.

cards.name: values, meaning and a good life (Part Three, chapter 10)
keys: how do i find my values
cards.what: Chapter 10 of Part Three is about values, meaning and a good life: what values are, how to find yours, what to do when two good things clash, and what old philosophy offers ordinary life today.
how: Think of a time you felt proud: which value were you living?
When two good things clash, choose for this week, not forever.
links: Chapter 10: Values, meaning and a good life

cards.name: healing after hurt (Part Three, chapter 11)
cards.what: Chapter 11 of Part Three is about healing after hurt: repair after small ruptures, apologies that land, what forgiveness is and is not, rebuilding trust, and when to get more help.
how: Repair small ruptures soon: name it, own your part, say what you will do.
Forgiveness is yours to give or not; it is not the same as trusting again.

cards.name: helping others well (Part Three, chapter 12)
keys: how do i help without taking over
how to help without taking over
cards.what: Chapter 12 of Part Three is about helping others well: ask what help is wanted, listen first, keep kind limits, help in a crisis, and look after yourself so you last.
how: Ask: “Do you want help, ideas, or just someone to listen?”
Keep a kind limit, so you can keep helping.

cards.name: closeness and love (Part Three, chapter 15)
cards.what: Chapter 15 of Part Three is about how closeness grows: love in many forms, intimacy as being known, feeling understood, attachment in adult love, and love across ages and relationship types.
how: Intimacy is being known, a little at a time.
Feeling understood matters more than agreeing.

cards.name: personality and temperament (Part Three, chapter 14)
cards.what: Chapter 14 of Part Three is about personality as dials, not boxes: the Big Five, temperament, introverts and extraverts, how people change with age, and living with different people.
how: Think of traits as dials, not boxes.
People do change with age, slowly, and mostly for the better.

cards.name: anger (Part Three, chapter 13)
keys: why do i get so angry
cards.what: Chapter 13 of Part Three is about anger: what it’s for, what it does in the body, steps for the hot minutes, why venting backfires, how to repair, and when anger becomes harm.
how: In the hot minutes: step away, breathe out slower than you breathe in, and come back to repair.
Anger is a signal that something matters. The repair is part of the skill.

cards.name: My weather today, quick mode (the 4-tap ladder check)
keys: where am i on the ladder
where am i on the ladder right now
cards.what: My weather today, quick mode, is a four-tap check (it used to be called Where am I right now?) on the nervous system ladder. It shows if you’re calm and connected, revved up, or running on empty, with what helps right now, a pause line to say, and when to talk again.
how: Open the ladder check and answer four quick taps.
Read what helps on your rung, right now.
If you’re revved up or shut down, use the pause line and pick a time to talk again.
links: Chapter 2: Stress and the nervous system

cards.name: Say no kindly (refusal scripts)
keys: how do i say no nicely
how do i say no kindly
how do i turn someone down nicely
how do i say no to extra work
cards.what: Say no kindly gives you copy-ready ways to say no. Pick a situation and a tone, and it offers three kind options, like “I’m full today”, “Not me, but let’s find who” or “Yes, just later”.
how: Pick the situation (family, friends, work, home) and a tone.
Copy one of the three ways to say no, and make it sound like you.
Say it once, kindly, without a long list of reasons.
Or use the Chat analyzer’s “Help me write it” mode: pick “Say no kindly”, and it checks your words at the end.
links: Chat analyzer: Help me write it (say no kindly)

cards.name: Effective communication: the complete, plain guide
keys: how to be a better listener
how can i be a better listener
how do we talk to each other better
how can we talk to each other better
how do i talk so people listen
how to talk so people listen
how do i get people to listen
cards.what: The communication guide brings together everything on this site about talking and listening. Good communication is shared meaning: what you meant and what they heard end up the same. It covers listening, saying what you need, timing, hard talks, repair, saying no, messages and texts, different wiring, and how it changes with partners, kids, family, friends, housemates and at work, with words you can say out loud and a 7-day practice plan.
how: Listen first, and check you got it before you answer: “So you mean…?”
Say one thing at a time: what happened, how you feel, and what you’d like.
Pick a calm moment. If either of you is flooded, pause and say when you’ll come back.
Repair mix-ups quickly. They’re normal.
If you feel afraid, it isn’t a communication problem: the safety page has help.
links: Effective communication: a complete, plain guide

cards.name: Bonding: how closeness grows
keys: how do we feel more connected
how can we feel more connected
cards.what: The Bonding page explains how closeness grows, from research on bids, responsiveness and play, with small ideas for partners, children and teens, friends, family, new families, housemates, coworkers and you. Small and often beats big and rare. It has a free idea picker, and ideas for bonding without eye contact or small talk.
how: Notice and answer the small ways people reach for you: a comment, a question, a look.
Do things side by side. Talking is optional.
Go at their pace. Closeness can be offered, never demanded.
Tap “Get a bonding idea” for one small thing to try today.

cards.name: Small wins, and turning hard feelings into fuel
keys: turn the hard stuff into fuel
turn a complaint into a request
how do i turn a complaint into a request
cards.what: Small wins build momentum: make the next step tiny, then notice, out loud, when it’s done. The same page shows how hard feelings are signals, not verdicts: ask what each one is pointing at, then turn a complaint into a kind, specific request and a worry into a plan. It has two small tools, Flip it and a done list.
how: Shrink the next step until it feels almost too easy, then do it.
Say it out loud when it’s done, or add it to the done list.
When a hard feeling comes up, ask what it’s pointing at.
Use Flip it to turn a complaint into a request, or a worry into a plan.
If it’s too heavy, a new way of looking at it is not the fix. Get support.

where do your studies come from
cards.what: The research page lists the studies, books and reviews this site leans on, each with what it found in plain words, how strong the evidence is, and a link to read more. It’s grouped by topic, from fairness and couples to stress, families, grief and minds that work differently. The site is self-help: it’s built from research, but the site itself hasn’t been tested in a trial.
how: Pick a topic, or use “Find a study” to search.
Check the label on each entry: strong, moderate, mixed, early, debated, or an idea rather than a test.
Follow the link to read the original if you’d like more.

cards.name: active listening
what: Active listening means following what the other person is trying to say, and letting them know you got it, before you add anything.
how: Give them your full attention: phone down, eyes up.
Say back what you heard, in your own words, without your opinion added.
Ask if you got it right. “Not quite” is good news: you’re getting closer.
Ask open questions: “What was the hardest part?”
Ask what they want: “Do you want ideas, or do you want me to just listen?”
Only then add your view. Understanding first, agreeing is optional.
script: So what I’m hearing is that you felt left to sort it on your own. Did I get that?
Do you want ideas, or do you want me to just listen?

_about_terms: terms: the site’s own words, defined plainly. The chat reads every term on /glossary.html (its plain definition, example and first link); entries here add terms or override one by id. idioms: sayings explained literally for “what does X mean?” questions. p lists the normalised phrases (lowercase, no apostrophes), lit what the words do not mean, m what people usually mean, tone how it usually sounds, plain a plain way to say it.

terms.d: The site uses “lens” in two different ways, and they mean different things:
list: Your lens (on Where your lens came from): the understandings about yourself, other people and what they owe you that you picked up growing up and still use without noticing. For example, “rest is earned” can feel like plain fact, until you notice it was your family’s rule.
The outside lens (on How it works): looking at your own situation calmly, as if from the outside, using what you wrote down over a few weeks instead of how it felt in the moment.
links: How it works: the outside lens

terms.d: Your lens is the set of understandings about yourself, other people and what they owe you that you picked up growing up and still use without noticing. It’s not the same as “the outside lens” on How it works.
terms.e: “Rest is earned” can feel like plain fact, until you notice it was your family’s rule.

terms.d: The outside lens means looking at your own situation calmly, as if from the outside: what actually happened, written down over a few weeks, instead of how it felt in the moment. It’s not the same as “your lens” from growing up.
terms.e: You believe you’re “just bad at mornings.” Written down for two weeks, the picture changes: mornings go wrong after late screens and no breakfast.
links: How it works: the outside lens

terms.d: In plain words: attachment theory, from the psychiatrist John Bowlby and the researcher Mary Ainsworth, says a child’s bond with the people who care for them is a basic need. A responsive carer works as a secure base (a safe place to explore from) and a safe haven (where the child comes back when frightened). Those early bonds shape, but don’t fix, what we expect from close relationships later, and adults’ patterns can change.
links: Attachment, trust and belonging (Part Three, Chapter 5)

terms.d: Autistic burnout is a deep, long-lasting exhaustion. Working with autistic adults, Dora Raymaker and colleagues (2020) described it as long-term exhaustion, loss of skills (like speech, planning or self-care) and lower tolerance of noise, light and other input. It comes from long stress without enough support, often after years of masking, and can last months. Rest, fewer demands and less masking help; pushing harder usually makes it worse.

idioms.lit: There’s no real room to read.
idioms.m: Notice how the people around you seem to feel, and fit what you say or do to that. For example, not telling a joke when everyone looks upset.
idioms.plain: Check how people are feeling before you speak.
idioms.tone: Usually a gentle nudge. Sometimes a mild telling-off.

idioms.lit: Nobody wants you to get hurt.

idioms.plain: I’m not sure yet. Ask me again on Friday.
